channel.title: AI Native Engine × AI Rendering 日报
channel.description: 每日精选：AI 原生引擎 / AI 渲染 / 游戏引擎 / 图形学（全文 + 中文导读）

item.title: 图形编程周报 #458：四元数 log/exp 的 SIMD 实现与本周图形精选 ｜ Graphics Programming Weekly - Issue 458 - October 11th, 2026
item.description:
一句话：本周图形论文与博客精选，头条是针对单位四元数的 SIMD 友好 log/exp 实现。

要点：

  • 单位四元数 log/exp 的可向量化实现，误差与吞吐都做了量化对比
  • 汇集本周新出的图形论文、引擎技术博客与工具更新
  • 每期按主题分组，是跟进图形前沿成本最低的一份周报

为什么值得看：动画与姿态系统里四元数插值无处不在，SIMD 化能直接吃到 CPU 端性能；其余条目可当每周技术雷达扫一遍。

中文摘要：本期周报汇集了 2026 年 10 月中旬的图形学论文与工程博客。头条是一份针对单位四元数 log/exp 的专用实现，采用 SIMD 友好写法，给出了误差与性能数据，适合动画、IK、姿态混合等高频插值场景直接采用。其余条目按渲染、几何、工具链分组，覆盖本周新论文与引擎侧技术分享。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：Graphics Programming Weekly（English）

Graphics Programming Weekly 458

Sun, Oct 11, 2026

weekly

presents specialized SIMD-friendly log and exp functions for unit quaternions

achieves error bounds comparable to standard-library implementations while avoiding full-turn angle ambiguity

introduces Reservoir Light Replay Backpropagation (ResLRB) for reverse-mode differentiable light tracing

compresses the adjoint graph during the primal pass with a streaming weighted reservoir

yields an unbiased gradient estimator whose peak memory is independent of path length

analyzes a frame of Hitman World of Assassination

covers G-buffer generation, tiled deferred lighting, cascaded shadows, screen-space ambient occlusion/reflections, volumetric fog and post-processing

maps GPU optimization instincts from graphics to large-language-model inference

benchmarks Qwen3 models on an RTX 3090 across quantization, Flash Attention, KV-cache compression and speculative decoding

shows optimization targeting the different bottlenecks

provides a self-study roadmap for learning graphics programming from free online resources

recommends C++, CMake, SDL alongside linear algebra, projective geometry and data structures

summarizes recent WebGPU and WGSL additions shipping in Chrome 155-156

highlights the fragment_depth extension, unaligned compressed textures, new linear color spaces and the snorm10-10-10-2 vertex format

introduces the upcoming bindless texture sampling support in WebGPU via GPUResourceTable

demonstrates a projected-decal emoji demo

compares bindless allocation against texture-array fallbacks and notes future heterogeneous resource tables

presents a real-time collision-detection framework for SDF-encoded geometry

combines temporal coherence caching with curvature-guided importance sampling to form sparse contact manifolds

runs complex scenes with thousands of rigid bodies

explains Metal dual-source blending, where a fragment shader emits a primary and secondary color for the blend unit

walks through using the technique to approximate sRGB-correct blending for Dear ImGui

concludes that programmable blending provides a more exact match on supported Apple Silicon GPUs

presents a plug-in acceleration suite for order-independent transparency

exploits spatial and temporal coherence through adaptive tiled sampling or variable-rate shading plus temporal reprojection

covers the development of a custom 2D lighting system in Unity for the cyberpunk game Glitch Hunt

applies data-oriented design principles to support hundreds of concurrent dynamic lights with minimal CPU overhead

details hand-drawn specular and bloom maps alongside reactive fog and rain systems

releases DxTimingCaptureLibrary, an open-source C++ helper for DirectX ETW events

exposes GPU timings, object lifetime, residency/paging, DirectStorage, pipeline compiles and PIX markers

provides samples for console logging, Perfetto tracing, D3D12 journal entries and memory visualization

updates meshoptimizer support for hierarchical clustered LOD using NVIDIA’s vk_lod_clusters sample

discusses meshopt compression, simplification improvements, error clamping and a new meshlet topology codec

shows the Zorah scene processing pipeline and foliage area-preservation heuristics

explains how Blender’s move from OpenGL to Vulkan and Metal exposed shader portability, compilation-time and legacy GLSL maintenance challenges

introduces Blender Shading Language (BSL), a C++ subset for sharing code between CPU and GPU

outlines plans to migrate more legacy shaders, expand C++ syntax support and consider binary formats as graphics standards evolve

explains how bgfx’s shaderc translates a GLSL dialect to many backend languages without its own AST

relies on the C preprocessor, textual patching and real target compilers such as FXC, DXC, Glslang and Tint

compares the approach with modern alternatives

presents a method that combines standard triangle mesh representations with per-pixel local raymarching to render displacement maps, volumetric effects, and self-shadowing on bone-animated meshes

preserves exisitng workflows and fallback to normal mapping

Thanks to for support of this series.

Nia Bickford

item.title: Walk in Envelopes：用可认证解界加速分支式球面游走 ｜ Walk in Envelopes: Efficient Branching Walk-on-Spheres via Certified Solution Bounds
item.description:
一句话：不去剪枝已有树，而是直接改造分支扩散过程，在临界分支率附近大幅降本且保持无偏。

要点：

  • 分支 Walk-on-Spheres 无需网格即可求解半线性 PDE，但分支率接近临界值时成本爆炸
  • 利用可认证的解界抑制繁殖，并引入可控终止
  • 在保持估计无偏的前提下显著降低成本

为什么值得看：体积渲染、参与介质、PDE 求解都用得到蒙特卡洛游走；这套「改造过程而非剪枝」的思路可以迁移到任何分支型采样器。

中文摘要：分支式球面游走（Branching Walk-on-Spheres）可以在无网格条件下求解半线性 PDE，但当分支率接近临界值时计算成本急剧增长。作者提出 Walk in Envelopes：利用可认证的解界来变换分支扩散过程本身，而不是事后剪枝已有树——通过抑制繁殖、引入受控终止，在保持无偏性的同时显著降低成本。这类方法可直接用于参与介质渲染与相关模拟。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

Walk in Envelopes: Efficient Branching Walk-on-Spheres via Certified Solution Bounds

Yunfeng Liao

, , , Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)ShenzhenGuangdongChina, Zhenhao Qiu

, , , Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)ShenzhenGuangdongChina, Xinyang Chen

, , , Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)ShenzhenGuangdongChina and Xiucheng Li

, , , Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)ShenzhenGuangdongChina© none

Walk in Envelopes (WiE) transforms branching WoS using certified lower and upper solution bounds. By reparameterizing the solution within a spatially varying envelope, WiE redistributes the original branching mechanism into splitting, return-0, and return-1 events, enabling early termination and pruning of redundant branches while preserving the target solution. The resulting computation trees are substantially smaller than those of conventional branching WoS.Figure 1. 1

Abstract.

Branching Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) solves semilinear PDEs without meshes, but its computational cost grows sharply near critical branching rates. We introduce (WiE), which uses certified solution bounds to transform branching diffusion rather than prune existing trees. The transformation suppresses reproduction, introduces controlled termination, and preserves unbiasedness with an envelope-dependent variance bound. We realize the transformed process through exact rejection sampling using standard screened WoS kernels, supported by certified spline envelopes and adaptive sampling and further prove that suitable harmonic envelopes yield bounded expected reproduction counts even as conventional BBM diverges.Walk in Envelopes

Walk-on-Spheres, Branching Brownian Motion, Semilinear PDEs, Certified Solution Bounds, Monte Carlo Methods

Keywords:

1.

Grid-free Monte Carlo methods have become an attractive alternative to mesh-based PDE solvers, enabling pointwise solution queries on complex domains without constructing a global discretization . While Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) efficiently resolves linear elliptic equations through boundary-hitting processes, extending this paradigm to semilinear PDEs requires handling nonlinear reactions. Branching Brownian motion (BBM) provides a natural probabilistic representation by replacing nonlinear terms with particle reproduction events . Combined with WoS, this yields a grid-free solver for semilinear equations. However, eliminating Brownian time discretization does not eliminate branching complexity: each offspring initiates additional walks, and the expected particle population diverges as the branching intensity approaches a critical spectral threshold. This makes otherwise valid stochastic representations increasingly expensive precisely in strongly nonlinear regimes.()

Sawhney and Crane, 2020

()

Agarwal and Claisse, 2020

A natural strategy is to exploit approximate solution information to terminate branches whose remaining contributions are sufficiently small. Yet such pruning requires reliable bounds on unresolved subtrees, whose evaluation can itself be expensive. Approximate bounds may also introduce bias, while tighter estimates do not necessarily offset their computation costs. More fundamentally, pruning acts on a branching process that has already been generated, rather than preventing unnecessary reproduction. This motivates a different question: can certified solution information be used to construct an equivalent stochastic process that branches less frequently, without sacrificing correctness?

We introduce (WiE), a branching WoS framework that transforms the stochastic representation using certified lower and upper solution envelopes. Given sub- and supersolutions $\ell\leq u\leq a$ , we normalize the unknown solution as $v=(u-\ell)/(a-\ell)$ . This induces a generalized Doob transform whose diffusion, reproduction, and termination mechanisms are determined by the envelope functions. For binary branching, the reproduction rate becomes $\lambda(a-\ell)$ , while envelope residuals introduce additional success and failure termination events. The resulting estimator remains unbiased and has variance bounded by $(a-\ell)^{2}/4$ . Moreover, we characterize its expected reproduction count through an elliptic equation, showing that a suitable harmonic envelope can keep this count uniformly bounded even as conventional BBM approaches its critical divergence threshold. Although branching-process transformations have established mathematical foundations , WiE develops them into a certified computational framework for semilinear PDE solving.Walk in Envelopes()

Engländer, 2007

The transformed process introduces spatially varying diffusion, which would ordinarily require simulating drifted trajectories. We avoid this difficulty by deriving an exact envelope-aware transition using the original screened WoS exit and Green kernels. Rejection sampling with certified local majorants realizes the transformed distribution without evaluating weighted kernel integrals. To obtain useful envelopes efficiently, we develop monotone refinement of cubic B-spline sub- and supersolutions, using Bernstein constraints to certify PDE inequalities throughout the domain by comparison principle. Adaptive screening, spatially localized rejection bounds, and lazy evaluation further reduce sampling overhead, while a spectral-workload criterion avoids unnecessary preprocessing in inexpensive regimes.

We evaluate WiE on four complex two-dimensional domains across branching intensities and accuracy requirements. Near criticality, WiE achieves $6.9$ – $16.2\times$ improvements in time–variance efficiency and $4.7$ – $14.6\times$ reductions in sampling time at matched accuracy, excluding one-time envelope construction. Its benefits increase with branching intensity, while a workload-aware fallback preserves the efficiency of conventional BBM in easier regimes. We additionally demonstrate extensions to projected walks on manifolds and semilinear parabolic equations.

Our main contributions are:

•

A certified envelope transformation of branching diffusion, with unbiased estimation, variance guarantees, and a spectral characterization of near-critical branching complexity.

•

An exact envelope-aware WoS sampler using existing screened kernels, without explicitly simulating transformed diffusion.

•

A practical solver combining certified spline-envelope refinement, efficient rejection sampling, and workload-aware fallback, with substantial near-critical acceleration.

2.

Branching Diffusions and Solution-Guided Transformations.

BBM represents semilinear reaction–diffusion PDEs, beginning with McKean’s Kolmogorov–Petrovskii–Piskunov representation . Branching-diffusion solvers extend to polynomial nonlinearities, gradient dependence via marked particles , and elliptic boundary-value problems on bounded domains , but face integrability and branching-cost restrictions under strong branching. Process transformations are well established: nonlinear $h$ -transforms alter both motion and reproduction , while measure changes and backbone decompositions characterize conditioned branching and near-critical behavior . These underpin solution-guided representations. Our computational realization uses certified sub- and supersolutions to obtain nonnegative branching and killing rates, with exact sphere-transition sampling requiring neither the unknown solution nor drifted-trajectory simulation.()

McKean, 1975

()

Henry-Labordère et al., 2019

()

Agarwal and Claisse, 2020

()

Engländer, 2007

(; )

Salisbury and Verzani, 2000

Harris et al., 2016

Monte Carlo Methods for Nonlinear Equations.

Monte Carlo solvers avoid global spatial discretization, but nested nonlinear expectations and recursive branching can sharply increase variance and work. Numerical branching methods handle polynomial nonlinear PDEs, subject to representation-dependent convergence and integrability . In graphics, accelerate nonlinear recursive light transport through nonlinear path filtering that reuses intermediate evaluations and neural radiance caching that learns them. For nonlinear radiative boundary conditions, combine Picard-style iteration with Monte Carlo PDE solvers. These reduce nonlinear integral-equation costs through reuse, approximation, or iteration. Instead, we retain a branching estimator but change its probability law: certified envelopes suppress reproduction, bound its range, and preserve its expectation under stated assumptions. We reduce sample-generation work rather than only accelerate or approximate an existing recursion.(; )

Henry-Labordère et al., 2019

Agarwal and Claisse, 2020

()

Tong and Hachisuka, 2025

()

Bao et al., 2026

Walk-on-Spheres and Grid-Free PDE Solvers.

WoS originated for Dirichlet problems and entered geometric computing as a grid-free elliptic PDE solver for point queries . Extensions handle spatially varying coefficients via null scattering , mixed Neumann–Dirichlet conditions via walk on stars , and boundary-integral transport via walk on boundary . Boundary-value caching reuses estimates across queries , differential WoS computes parameter derivatives , and projected walks solve surface PDEs . These advances mainly address linear PDE representations, boundary handling, or stochastic-estimate reuse. For semilinear PDEs, sphere jumps eliminate Brownian time discretization but not branching-tree growth. We target this remaining bottleneck through certified semilinear bounds and a transformed process with weighted exit and interior events sampled using the original screened WoS kernels.()

Muller, 1956

()

Sawhney and Crane, 2020

()

Sawhney et al., 2022

()

Sawhney et al., 2023

()

Sugimoto et al., 2023

()

Miller et al., 2023

()

Miller et al., 2024

()

Sugimoto et al., 2024a

3.

3.1.

Branching Brownian motion (BBM) provides a stochastic representation of semilinear elliptic PDEs by interpreting nonlinear reactions as particle branching events. Consider $F(u):=\mathcal{L}u+\lambda(P(u)-u)=0$ with Dirichlet condition $u|_{\partial\Omega}=g$ , where $P(u)=\sum_{k=0}^{K}p_{k}u^{k}$ is the offspring generating function and $\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{2}\Delta$ . Each particle follows Brownian motion until either reaching the boundary or branching into $k$ independent offspring with probability $p_{k}$ at an exponential rate $\lambda$ . The solution is recovered as $u(x)=\mathbb{E}[\prod_{i\in\mathcal{T}}g(X_{i})]$ , where $\mathcal{T}$ is the terminal leaves.

For probabilistic semilinear elliptic PDEs, Dirichlet values naturally lie in $[0,1]$ . For example, $g(y)\in[0,1]$ may specify the success probability of a particle absorbed at $y$ , in which case $u(x)$ gives the probability that every terminal particle succeeds. This interpretation follows directly from the BBM representation $u(x)=\mathbb{E}[\prod_{i\in\mathcal{L}}g(X_{i})]$ , and ensures $0\leq u\leq 1$ .

Branching WoS accelerates this process by replacing Brownian trajectories with sphere transitions. At each particle position $x$ , let $B=B(x,r)\subset\Omega$ be the largest inscribed ball, and denote by $H_{\lambda}$ and $G_{\lambda}$ its screened exit and Green kernels, respectively. Conditioning on whether the particle exits the ball before branching yields the integral equation induced by total expectation:

(1) $u(x)=\int_{\partial B}H_{\lambda}(x,\mathrm{d}y)\,u(y)+\lambda\int_{B}G_{\lambda}(x,y)\sum_{k=0}^{K}p_{k}u(y)^{k}\,\mathrm{d}y.$

Specifically, the exit probability is $q_{B}=\int_{\partial B}H_{\lambda}(x,\mathrm{d}y)=1/I_{0}(r\sqrt{2\lambda})$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , where $I_{0}$ denotes the modified Bessel function. With probability $q_{B}$ , the particle jumps uniformly to $\partial B$ and continues walking; otherwise, an interior branching location $Y$ is sampled with density $\lambda G_{\lambda}(x,y)/(1-q_{B})$ , and $k\sim(p_{k})$ offspring are added to the active particle queue at $Y$ . The procedure repeats until all particles reach the domain boundary or terminate with zero offspring, producing one Monte Carlo sample from the product of terminal values. Thus, although WoS eliminates explicit trajectory discretization, each sphere transition still requires a branching decision, while every offspring introduces additional walks that must be maintained and evaluated. Canonical results show that BWoS crashes when the particle splitting rate surpasses the boundary-absorbing speed, i.e., $\lambda>\lambda_{1}$ where $\lambda_{1}$ is the least non-negative eigenvalue of $-\mathcal{L}$ in $\Omega$ .

3.2.

Although WoS eliminates explicit Brownian trajectory discretization, its computational cost still grows with the branching tree. The expected cumulative particle population becomes unbounded as $\lambda$ approaches the principal Dirichlet eigenvalue $\lambda_{1}$ associated with $\Omega$ , motivating the early termination of subtrees whose remaining contributions can be bounded. Let $\tau$ denote the first Brownian exit time from $\Omega$ , and $h(x)=\mathbb{E}_{x}[g(B_{\tau})]$ the harmonic extension of $g$ . Several bounds follow directly from the BBM representation and its associated linear equations as Theorem .

3.1

Theorem 3.1 (Probabilistic Solution Bounds).

For $0<\lambda<\lambda_{1},P(u)=u^{2}$ and $0\leq g\leq 1$ , the solution of $F(u)=0$ with $u|{\partial\Omega}=g$ satisfies ${\max}\{L_{0}(x),L_{1}(x),L_{2}(x)\}\leq u(x)\leq U(x),$

where $U=h$ , and $L_{0}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{x}[e^{-\lambda\tau}g(B\tau)]$ , $L_{1}(x)=1-\mathbb{E}_{x}[e^{\lambda\tau}(1-g(B_{\tau}))]$ , $L_{2}(x)=h(x)-\tfrac{\lambda}{4}\mathbb{E}_{x}[\tau]$ .

Proof.

Since $F(u)=0$ implies $\mathcal{L}u=\lambda u(1-u)\geq 0$ , the maximum principle gives $u\leq h=U$ . For $L_{0}$ , restrict the BBM expectation to trajectories reaching the boundary before their first branching event; all omitted products are nonnegative, yielding $u\geq\mathbb{E}_{x}[e^{-\lambda\tau}g(B_{\tau})]$ . For $L_{1}$ , let $q=1-u$ . Then $\mathcal{L}q+\lambda q=\lambda q^{2}\geq 0$ . The Feynman–Kac formula gives $q(x)=\mathbb{E}_{x}[e^{\lambda\tau}(1-g(B_{\tau}))]-\lambda\mathbb{E}_{x}[\int_{0}^{\tau}e^{\lambda t}q(B_{t})^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t]$ , hence $u\geq L_{1}$ . Finally, Dynkin’s formula gives $h-u=\lambda\mathbb{E}_{x}[\int_{0}^{\tau}u(B_{t})(1-u(B_{t}))\,\mathrm{d}t]$ . Since $u(1-u)\leq 1/4$ , we obtain $u\geq L_{2}$ .

∎

These bounds enable early termination of unresolved branching subtrees. Suppose the completed leaves contribute a product $\omega\in[0,1]$ , while the active frontier contains particles at $x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}$ . By conditional independence, their remaining expected contribution is $R=\omega\prod_{i=1}^{m}u(x_{i})$ . With bounds $L\leq u\leq U$ immediately yield

(2) $B^{-}:=\omega\prod_{i=1}^{m}L(x_{i})\leq R\leq\omega\prod_{i=1}^{m}U(x_{i}):=B^{+}.$

Thus, whenever $B^{+}-B^{-}\leq 2\varepsilon$ , the remaining tree can be pruned and replaced by $(B^{-}+B^{+})/2$ , introducing at most $\varepsilon$ absolute bias in the final expectation, since the conditional expected contribution lies within $[B^{-},B^{+}]$ .

Pruning speedup relative to vanilla WoS–BBM (dashed $1\times$ ) across branching rates $\beta$ , for constant, $P_{2}$ , $P_{10}$ , and binary-hemisphere boundary data (mean $0.5$ ).Figure 2.

Despite their validity, these bounds incur evaluation overhead and exhibit strongly case-dependent efficiency (Fig. ). $L_{0}$ ignores branched trajectories, $L_{1}$ deteriorates with large boundary deficits, while $L_{2}$ relies on the worst-case bound $u(1-u)\leq 1/4$ . Consequently, $L_{2}$ generally performs best on smooth boundaries, whereas discontinuous binary data defeats most pruning with binary boundary condition. Combining all bounds often increases overhead without proportional savings. This motivates certified envelopes that directly reduce branching rather than repeatedly pruning existing trees.

2

3.3.

The preceding pruning strategy uses solution bounds to terminate subtrees after they have been generated, but does not alter the underlying branching dynamics. We instead construct an equivalent branching process whose reproduction and termination rates are determined directly by certified solution envelopes. This can be understood as a generalized Doob’s $h$ -transform, where the envelope width acts as the transforming function.

For $F(u)=0$ , let $\ell$ and $a$ be certified sub- and supersolutions satisfying $0\leq\ell\leq u\leq a\leq 1$ , $F(\ell)\geq 0$ , and $F(a)\leq 0$ . Define the domain envelop width $d:=a-\ell>0$ , the normalized solution $v=(u-\ell)/d\in[0,1]$ , and the nonnegative residuals $r_{\ell}=F(\ell)$ and $r_{a}=-F(a)$ . By substituting $u=\ell+dv$ and expanding the offspring generating function, we obtain

$P(\ell+dv)=P(\ell)+\sum_{j=1}^{K}C_{j}v^{j},\qquad C_{j}=\frac{P^{(j)}(\ell)}{j!}d^{j}\geq 0.$

The key is that the transformation changes not only the diffusion operator but also the branching mechanism into four parts – drifted diffusion $\mathcal{L}^{d}v$ , reduced branching $\sum_{j=2}^{K}{\lambda C_{j}(v^{j}-v)}/{d}$ , returning one $r_{c}(1-v)/d$ and zero (being killed) $-{r_{a}}v/{d}$ in the theorem below.

Theorem 3.2 (Generalized Envelope Branching).

With certified envelopes satisfying the conditions above and well-defined and integrable transformed branching process, $v=(u-\ell)/d$ satisfies

(3) $\displaystyle 0=\mathcal{L}^{d}v+\sum_{j=2}^{K}\frac{\lambda C_{j}}{d}(v^{j}-v)+\frac{r_{\ell}}{d}(1-v)-\frac{r_{a}}{d}v,$

where $\mathcal{L}^{d}=\mathcal{L}+\nabla\log d\cdot\nabla$ . Consequently, the equivalent process branches into $j\geq 2$ offspring at rate $\lambda C_{j}/d$ , terminates successfully at rate $r_{\ell}/d$ , and terminates unsuccessfully at rate $r_{a}/d$ . If $W\in[0,1]$ is its terminal-product estimator, then $Z(x)=\ell(x)+d(x)W$ is unbiased $\mathbb{E}[Z(x)]=u(x)$ and

(4) $\operatorname{Var}[Z(x)]\leq(u(x)-\ell(x))(a(x)-u(x))\leq{d(x)^{2}}/{4}.$

Proof.

The product rule gives $\mathcal{L}(dv)=d\mathcal{L}^{d}v+v\mathcal{L}d$ , where $\mathcal{L}^{d}v=d^{-1}[\mathcal{L}(dv)-v\mathcal{L}d]$ . Since $F(a)-F(\ell)=-r_{a}-r_{\ell}$ and $P(a)-P(\ell)=\sum_{j=1}^{K}C_{j}$ , we have $\mathcal{L}d-\lambda d=-r_{\ell}-r_{a}-\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{K}C_{j}$ . Substituting these identities into $F(\ell+dv)=0$ yields $d\mathcal{L}^{d}v+r_{\ell}(1-v)-r_{a}v+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{K}C_{j}(v^{j}-v)=0$ . The $j=1$ term vanishes, giving Eq. (). Its nonnegative rates define the stated branching process, with boundary payoff $(g-\ell)/d\in[0,1]$ . The branching representation gives $\mathbb{E}[W]=v$ , hence $\mathbb{E}[Z]=u$ . Finally, $Z\in[\ell,a]$ implies $\mathbb{E}[(Z-\ell)(a-Z)]\geq 0$ , which yields Eq. ().

For binary branching, this reduces to $\left[-\mathcal{L}+\lambda(1-2a)\right]H=\lambda d^{2}.$ Thus, the transformation changes both the source of branching work and the elliptic operator governing its propagation. In particular, narrowing the envelope suppresses the quadratic source term, while the upper envelope controls the effective reproduction potential. These effects explain how WiE can reduce branching complexity even when conventional BBM approaches its critical regime. Also, there exists a harmonic envelope such that the cost of WiE keeps finite as the splitting rate approaches the divergence limit of vanilla WoS in theory as Theorem  reveals.

Theorem 3.4 (Bounded near-critical branching with harmonic envelopes).

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a bounded, connected $C^{2,\alpha}$ domain, and let $\lambda_{1}>0$ be the principal Dirichlet eigenvalue of $-\mathcal{L}$ , where $\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{2}\Delta$ . Suppose $g\in C^{2,\alpha}(\partial\Omega)$ satisfies $0\leq g\leq 1$ , $g\not\equiv 0$ , and $g\not\equiv 1$ . Let $h$ be its harmonic extension, $\mathcal{L}h=0$ in $\Omega$ and $h=g$ on $\partial\Omega$ . For the binary branching equation $\mathcal{L}u+\lambda(u^{2}-u)=0$ , choose the certified envelopes $\ell=0$ and $a=h$ . Then the expected reproduction count $m_{\lambda}$ of the transformed process satisfies

(7) $\sup_{0<\lambda<\lambda_{1}}|m_{\lambda}|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}<\infty.$

In contrast, the expected reproduction count $m_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{BBM}}$ of conventional binary BBM diverges as $\lambda\uparrow\lambda_{1}$ : for every fixed $x\in\Omega$ , $m_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{BBM}}(x)=\Theta((\lambda_{1}-\lambda)^{-1})$ .

Proof.

The strong maximum principle gives $00$ in the interior. By Lemma 3.3, $H_{\lambda}:=hm_{\lambda}$ solves

(8) $A_{\lambda}H_{\lambda}=\lambda h^{2},\qquad H_{\lambda}|{\partial\Omega}=0,\qquad A\lambda=-\mathcal{L}-\lambda+2\lambda(1-h).$

We first show that $A_{\lambda}$ has a spectral gap uniform up to $\lambda_{1}$ . At $\lambda=\lambda_{1}$ , its quadratic form is

(9) $\langle f,A_{\lambda_{1}}f\rangle=\underbrace{\|\nabla f\|_{2}^{2}/2-\lambda_{1}\|f\|_{2}^{2}}_{\geq 0}+2\lambda_{1}\int_{\Omega}(1-h)f^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x.$

If its lowest eigenvalue were zero, equality would force $f$ to be a multiple of the positive first Dirichlet eigenfunction $\phi_{1}$ and simultaneously $\int_{\Omega}(1-h)f^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x=0$ , contradicting $1-h>0$ in $\Omega$ . Hence $\kappa:=\lambda_{\min}(A_{\lambda_{1}})>0$ . Writing $t=\lambda/\lambda_{1}$ gives $A_{\lambda}=(1-t)(-\mathcal{L})+tA_{\lambda_{1}}$ , so the min–max principle yields

(10) $\lambda_{\min}(A_{\lambda})\geq(1-t)\lambda_{1}+t\kappa\geq\min{\lambda_{1},\kappa}>0.$

Uniform invertibility and standard Dirichlet elliptic estimates therefore imply $|H_{\lambda}|{C^{1}(\overline{\Omega})}\leq C$ , with $C$ independent of $\lambda\in(0,\lambda_{1})$ . Since $H\lambda=0$ on $\partial\Omega$ , $|H_{\lambda}(x)|\leq C,\mathrm{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)$ . On the other hand, positivity of $h$ in the interior, the Hopf boundary lemma at points where $g=0$ , and compactness of $\partial\Omega$ imply $h(x)\geq c,\mathrm{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)$ for some $c>0$ . Thus $m_{\lambda}=H_{\lambda}/h\leq C/c$ throughout $\Omega$ , proving the bound.

For conventional BBM, $(-\mathcal{L}-\lambda)m_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{BBM}}=\lambda$ with zero Dirichlet boundary data. The isolated principal-eigenvalue resolvent expansion gives

(11) $m_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{BBM}}(x)=\frac{\lambda_{1}\langle 1,\phi_{1}\rangle\phi_{1}(x)}{\lambda_{1}-\lambda}+O_{x}(1),\qquad\lambda\uparrow\lambda_{1},$

where $|\phi_{1}|_{2}=1$ . This proves the stated divergence.

12

The remaining challenge is sampling this distribution without evaluating its weighted integrals. Although Eq. () provides the normalizing constant $d(x)$ , directly sampling a density proportional to $H_{\lambda}d$ or $G_{\lambda}\omega_{I}$ would require a new sampler for each spatially varying envelope. Instead, we use rejection sampling to recover these densities from the original WoS proposals.

14

Specifically, the target exit and interior transition measures are proportional to $H_{\lambda}(x,\mathrm{d}y)d(y)$ and $\lambda G_{\lambda}(x,y)\omega_{I}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y$ , respectively. We therefore introduce two certified constants $M_{E}\geq\sup_{\partial B}d$ and $M_{I}\geq\sup_{B}\omega_{I}$ to dominate these weighted measures by distributions that are already straightforward to sample. Let $q_{B}=\int_{\partial B}H_{\lambda}(x,\mathrm{d}y)$ denote the original sphere-exit probability. The corresponding proposal masses are $q_{B}M_{E}$ for exits and $(1-q_{B})M_{I}$ for interior events, giving the computable normalization $Q_{B}=q_{B}M_{E}+(1-q_{B})M_{I}$ .

We first choose an exit proposal with probability $q_{B}M_{E}/Q_{B}$ , otherwise an interior proposal. Its position $Y$ is drawn from $H_{\lambda}/q_{B}$ or $\lambda G_{\lambda}/(1-q_{B})$ , respectively, and accepted with probability $d(Y)/M_{E}$ or $\omega_{I}(Y)/M_{I}$ . For example, the joint probability measure of proposing and accepting an exit at $y$ is $\frac{q_{B}M_{E}}{Q_{B}}\frac{H_{\lambda}(x,\mathrm{d}y)}{q_{B}}\frac{d(y)}{M_{E}}=\frac{H_{\lambda}(x,\mathrm{d}y)d(y)}{Q_{B}}.$

Similarly, the accepted interior measure is $\lambda G_{\lambda}(x,y)\omega_{I}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y/Q_{B}$ . Their total mass is $d(x)/Q_{B}$ by Eq. (). Conditioning on acceptance therefore divides both measures by $d(x)/Q_{B}$ , recovering exactly the target transition probabilities. Thus, the accpetance rate is $d(x)/Q_{B}$ and rejected candidates can simply be resampled. Notice that neither the target normalization $d(x)$ nor any weighted Green integral needs to be evaluated during sampling.

4.1.

The transformation admits many certified envelopes with different computational costs. We construct tight, reusable bounds for full-field evaluation through four steps: a comparison principle certifies bounds from PDE residuals and boundary conditions; query-weighted envelope width approximates the intractable time–variance objective; conservative affine constraints monotonically refine an initially feasible pair; and cubic B-splines with cellwise Bernstein constraints reduce continuous certification to finite-dimensional linear programs. Certification is preserved throughout, while preprocessing is amortized across repeated queries.

Lemma 4.1 (Comparison Principle for Certified Envelopes).

For a bounded Lipschitz domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , assume $\lambda\geq 0$ and $\lambda\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\allowbreak(P^{\prime}(s)-1)<\lambda_{1}.$ Suppose $u,\ell,a\in C^{2}(\Omega)\cap C(\overline{\Omega})\cap H^{1}(\Omega)$ take values in $[0,1]$ and satisfy $F(u)=0,F(\ell)\geq 0,F(a)\leq 0$ and

$\ell\leq u\leq a$ on $\partial\Omega$ . Then

$\ell\leq u\leq a$ throughout $\Omega$ .

Proof.

We first prove $\ell\leq u$ . Set $w=\ell-u$ . Since

$F(\ell)-F(u)\geq 0$ , subtracting the two PDE residuals gives $\mathcal{L}w+\lambda\bigl(P(\ell)-P(u)-w\bigr)\geq 0.$ To rewrite the nonlinear difference as a term proportional to $w$ ,

apply the fundamental theorem of calculus pointwise:

(18) $P(\ell(x))-P(u(x))=\int_{u(x)}^{\ell(x)}P^{\prime}(s)\,\mathrm{d}s=w(x)\int_{0}^{1}P^{\prime}\bigl(u(x)+tw(x)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t.$

Define the bounded coefficient $q(x)=\int_{0}^{1}P^{\prime}\bigl(u(x)+tw(x)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t.$ Because $0\leq u,\ell\leq 1$ , every argument of $P^{\prime}$ lies in $[0,1]$ , and thus

(19) $\lambda(q(x)-1)\leq\lambda\sup_{s\in[0,1]}(P^{\prime}(s)-1)<\lambda_{1}.$

It follows that $\frac{1}{2}\Delta w+\lambda(q(x)-1)w\geq 0,\qquad w\leq 0\quad\text{on }\partial\Omega.$ We now justify the maximum-principle step rather than assuming it.

Let $w_{+}=\max\{w,0\}$ . Since $w\leq 0$ on the boundary and

$w\in H^{1}(\Omega)$ , we have $w_{+}\in H_{0}^{1}(\Omega)$ . Multiplying the

last differential inequality by $w_{+}$ and integrating by parts gives

(20) $0\leq-\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla w_{+}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x+\lambda\int_{\Omega}(q(x)-1)w_{+}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x.$

Consequently,

(21) $\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla w_{+}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\leq c_{*}\int_{\Omega}w_{+}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad c_{*}:=\lambda\sup_{s\in[0,1]}(P^{\prime}(s)-1).$

The variational characterization of the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of

$-\frac{1}{2}\Delta$ states that, for any $\varphi\in H_{0}^{1}(\Omega)$ , $\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla\varphi|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\geq\lambda_{1}\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x.$ Applying this inequality to $\varphi=w_{+}$ yields $(\lambda_{1}-c_{*})\int_{\Omega}w_{+}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\leq 0.$

Since $\lambda_{1}-c_{*}>0$ , we obtain $w_{+}=0$ , hence $\ell\leq u$ .

To prove $u\leq a$ , repeat the same argument with $w=u-a$ .

Indeed, $F(u)-F(a)\geq 0$ , $w\leq 0$ on the boundary, and $P(u)-P(a)=w\int_{0}^{1}P^{\prime}\bigl(a+t(u-a)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t.$

The same upper bound on the resulting zero-order coefficient

and the same energy argument show $(u-a)_{+}=0$ . Thus

$\ell\leq u\leq a$ in $\Omega$ .

Work-aware envelope optimization.

Let $\mathcal{Q}\subset\Omega$ denote the evaluation region and let $T_{\ell,a}(x)$ and $V_{\ell,a}(x)$ be the expected runtime and estimator variance induced by a certified envelope pair $(\ell,a)$ . For full-field evaluation, the ideal envelopes minimize the total cost of reaching a prescribed accuracy $\int_{\mathcal{Q}}T_{\ell,a}(x)V_{\ell,a}(x)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(x)$ . Here $\mu$ describes the distribution of evaluation queries. The objective reflects the time–variance cost of independent Monte Carlo evaluation, but is difficult to optimize directly because $T_{\ell,a}$ depends on the entire transformed branching process.

Fortunately, the envelope width $d=a-\ell$ provides a tractable surrogate. From Eq. (), the transformed reproduction coefficients are $C_{j}=P^{(j)}(\ell)d^{j}/j!$ . In particular, for binary branching, the probability mass associated with reproduction is proportional to $d^{2}$ . Moreover, Eq. () bounds the estimator variance by $d^{2}/4$ . These observations motivate minimizing the domain-averaged envelope width which replaces $T_{\ell,a}(x)V_{\ell,a}(x)$ , yielding

This objective seeks a single pair of reusable envelopes rather than independently optimizing bounds at each evaluation point. While width reduction does not guarantee a proportional runtime improvement, it simultaneously suppresses higher-order reproduction terms and tightens the estimator’s variance bound.

Finite-dimensional certified optimization.

We represent the envelopes using cubic B-splines,

$\ell(x)=\sum_{i}c_{i}^{\ell}\phi_{i}(x)$ and

$a(x)=\sum_{i}c_{i}^{a}\phi_{i}(x)$ , with their coefficients as optimization variables. Although Eq. () is affine in the corrections, it imposes infinitely many spatial constraints. The following theorem provides a finite-dimensional certification. On each spline cell, we express the affine residuals and ordering constraints in the Bernstein basis, enforcing nonnegativity of their coefficients; range and polynomial boundary constraints are handled analogously. These finitely many sufficient linear inequalities certify the PDE constraints throughout the domain while preserving monotone envelope refinement.

28

For nonrectangular domains, we may restrict these certificates to a decomposition of each cell intersected with $\Omega$ , using tensor-product or triangular Bernstein bases on the resulting pieces. This changes the sufficient finite constraints, while retaining the same globally $C^{2}$ spline representation and continuous PDE inequalities on $\Omega$ . Therefore, the resulting refinement is a linear program with continuous, rather than pointwise, certification. The Bernstein constraints yields a conservative feasible set. The envelopes are constructed once and reused across full-field evaluations, amortizing their preprocessing cost over all queries.

4.2.

Although the envelope transformation reduces branching complexity, sampling its spatially varying transition weights introduces additional overhead. We employ three complementary optimizations to reduce this cost while preserving the exact transition law.

Adaptive screening.

The screened-kernel representation allows an adjustable parameter $\mu\in[0,\lambda]$ . Using Eq. (), the interior weight $W_{\mu}=\lambda\omega_{I}-(\lambda-\mu)d$ , yielding

3

(29) $\displaystyle W_{\mu}=r_{\ell}+r_{a}+\lambda\sum_{j=2}^{K}C_{j}+[\mu-\lambda+\lambda P^{\prime}(\ell)]d.$

This decomposition shows that changing $\mu$ affects only the single-offspring continuation weight, leaving termination and genuine reproduction weights unchanged. Their nonnegativity is preserved by choosing $\mu_{B}=\lambda\max\{0,1-P^{\prime}(\underline{\ell}_{B})\}$ , where $\underline{\ell}_{B}$ is a certified lower bound over the sphere. A smaller $\mu_{B}$ increases the sphere-exit probability, potentially reducing expensive interior proposals without altering the represented solution.

Spatially adaptive majorants.

Instead of using global rejection bounds, we independently bound the exit and interior weights by $M_{E}\geq\sup_{\partial B}d$ and $M_{I}\geq\sup_{B}W_{\mu}$ . Their proposal masses are $q_{\mu}M_{E}$ and $m_{\mu}M_{I}$ , where $q_{\mu}=\int_{\partial B}H_{\mu}$ and $m_{\mu}=\int_{B}G_{\mu}$ . The corresponding acceptance probabilities are $d(y)/M_{E}$ and $W_{\mu}(y)/M_{I}$ . We obtain tight local bounds from the spline cells intersecting each sphere and accelerate their aggregation using range-minimum/maximum queries (RMQ), reducing rejection without changing the accepted distribution.

Lazy evaluation.

Even with tighter proposals, computing the exact envelope weights for every candidate is unnecessary. We first compare the rejection threshold against inexpensive local lower and upper bounds: candidates are accepted or rejected immediately when these bounds determine the outcome, and full spline evaluation is performed only otherwise. Green-kernel sampling is deferred until an interior proposal is selected, while reusable kernel quantities are cached. Thus, most inexpensive decisions avoid the cost of exact weight evaluation, and the savings accumulate across repeated transitions in the branching tree.

Bottom: unconnected points show the normalized scale $A_{\mathrm{break}}/A$ , where $A_{\mathrm{break}}=(Q_{\mathrm{break}}/\varepsilon^{2})\rho/(1-\rho)$ , across five target accuracies. The horizontal dashed line marks $A_{\mathrm{break}}/A=1$ . Their near-critical concentration around one motivates the empirical rule $\rho\geq 0.8$ and $\mathcal{W}\geq 10^{8}$ . Vertical dotted lines mark $\rho=0.8$ ; the shaded region in the top panel indicates $\rho\geq 0.8$ . Costs combine recorded preprocessing with equal-RMSE sampling estimates.Figure 5.

Spectral-workload fallback.

Envelope construction incurs a one-time cost that may outweigh its sampling benefits. Motivated by the near-critical BBM work scaling $(1-\rho)^{-1}$ , where $\rho=\lambda(P^{\prime}(1)-1)/\lambda_{1}<1$ , we define a spectral-workload indicator for $Q$ queries at target RMSE $\varepsilon$ :

(30) $\mathcal{W}=\frac{Q}{\varepsilon^{2}}\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}.$

We activate WiE only when $\rho\geq\rho_{0}$ and $\mathcal{W}\geq A$ , with $\rho_{0}=0.8$ and $A=10^{8}$ calibrated empirically across four scenes (Figure ). This pilot-free criterion avoids unnecessary preprocessing, while imperfect fallback decisions affect efficiency but not correctness.

5

5.

Our proposed WiE algorithm is evaluated in four non-trivial 2D scenes against canonical branching WoS. The results are illustrated in Figure  and the its speedup effects are evaluated with different branching rates. In Table , it is clear that WiE naturally appears insignificant with low splitting rate and thus the extra processing cost overwhelms its variance advantage per sample; while its merit become explicit as $\beta/\lambda_{1}$ grows, it strongly suppresses the splitting rate in simulation by being enveloped, which is consistent across all scenarios. Besides, WiE also achieves the same accuracy using much less time than vanilla branching WoS in high splitting scenes as in Table .

6

1

2

Two-dimensional fields in four domains. Reference and WiE use 1,000 and 600 samples per query, respectively. The reference is itself a Monte Carlo estimate; these are not equal-time results. Geometry and queries share the same rigid $180^{\circ}$ rotation, and all fields use the same color range. Nearest-query display preserves the original values.Figure 6. Upright Engine, Flask, Clover, and Lock fields, each with reference and WiE side by side.

Efficiency across branching intensities. Single-sample variances are averaged over query points; the BBM and WiE work columns report $10^{3}\sum_{i}t_{i}\operatorname{Var}[Z_{i}]$ (lower is better), where $t_{i}$ is the CPU time measured at 256 samples per query. Speedup is the ratio of these work measures. All results average three seeds; envelope preprocessing is excluded.Table 1.

Equal-accuracy cost under a fixed near-critical branching intensity $\rho=\beta/\widehat{\lambda}_{1}=0.99$ . We vary the target stochastic RMSE $\varepsilon$ over one order of magnitude; $N$ is the number of independent trees per query. CPU time (seconds) is summed over 48 fixed queries and averaged across three seeds, excluding envelope preprocessing. Sample budgets are variance-calibrated, and speedup is the ratio of measured CPU costs.Table 2.

Envelope construction ablation.

We compare three certified constructions with the same $6\times 6$ bicubic basis: optimizes the upper and then lower envelope separately, minimizes their width together, and further tightens the joint solution by certified nonlinear iterations. The archived three-update configuration in Figure  shows that joint optimization improves width over sequential fitting, while refinement additionally reduces it by $5.5\%$ on Engine and $7.2\%$ on Flask without increasing spline resolution. Gains on Lock and Clover are negligible, and tighter envelopes do not uniformly imply lower sampling work. Thus, iteration can improve a fixed representation, but is not a universal substitute for increasing its resolution.sequential LPjoint LPmonotone refinement

7

Construction ablation at $\rho=0.98$ : (a) mean certified envelope width and (b) sampling time–variance cost relative to refined WiE. All methods use the same $6\times 6$ spline basis. The unavailable Flask sequential certificate is marked N/A.Figure 7.

Spline resolution.

Table (a) examines spatial resolution and geometric certification. The earlier implementation certifies the entire bounding square, including regions outside the PDE domain and inside holes. We instead clip certificate cells to the original polygon: intact or axis-aligned pieces use tensor-product Bernstein coefficients, and oblique pieces use triangular Bernstein coefficients. The envelopes remain globally $C^{2}$ cubic B-splines. We keep the same boundary data, offspring laws, and $\rho=\lambda(P^{\prime}(1)-1)/\widehat{\lambda}_{1}=0.98$ . For all six non-square domains, we transfer the same $k=6$ joint initialization exactly to $k=12$ and $24$ before refinement, so the resolution comparison does not change the initial functions. Both coefficient vectors are restricted to $[-2,2]$ to suppress large, weakly constrained exterior modes. This extension constraint is additional to the certified range and PDE conditions inside $\Omega$ .

3

Refinement iterations.

We allow up to 12 updates, retaining $d\geq 0.003$ and the upper-correction limit $0.075$ . We stop after two successive width reductions below $10^{-6}$ , or return the last valid pair when the LP budget or numerical checks fail; the actual accepted count is reported. If the full polynomial LP accepts no update, we retry from the same initialization using conservative cellwise scalar bounds on the residuals and $P^{\prime}$ ; both attempts are included in construction cost. Table (b) tests the returned pairs with fixed queries, sample count, seeds, and rejection-bound grid. At $k=24$ , the six non-square cases reduce mean width by 53–87% relative to the earlier coarse result. Relative to their common initialization, their sampling time–variance efficiency improves by $2.06$ – $23.13\times$ , while additional construction costs $298$ – $600$ CPU seconds. Thus finer envelopes improve sampling in these tests, but need sufficient reuse to offset preprocessing. The L-shaped case attains a smaller mean width at $k=12$ than at $k=24$ ; the latter uses the conservative fallback, and these finite-budget results do not imply monotonic improvement with resolution. These results diagnose envelope construction rather than changing the variable transformation underlying WiE. All cases use the general-PGF kernel; Figure  retains the earlier specialized binary implementation.

4

7

Near-critical spline construction at $\rho=0.98$ . (a) Mean width $\bar{d}$ on the fixed construction queries. is the earlier full-box $k=6$ refinement; the other columns use certificates restricted to the geometric domain. All resolutions start from exactly the same $k=6$ joint envelope, transferred by knot insertion, with $(k+3)^{2}$ coefficients per side. We sweep $k=6,12,24$ on all six non-square domains; the three square cases remain $k=6$ controls. Refinement allows at most 12 updates, with a two-update width-plateau threshold of $10^{-6}$ . A dagger indicates termination by the LP budget or numerical failure, rather than convergence. $j_{*}$ counts accepted updates at the resolution used in (b). At $k=24$ , the scalar fallback is used for L-shaped, Two holes.Table 3. Box

Sampling optimization ablation.

Figure  isolates Bernstein squeeze and RMQ using the same certified envelopes and random paths ( $\rho=0.98$ ). Squeeze reduces full spline evaluations from $14$ – $17$ to $2.5$ – $4.7$ per root sample; disabling it increases CPU time by $6.9$ – $15.6\%$ . Disabling both optimizations increases CPU by $9$ – $16\%$ . RMQ alone offers limited and sometimes negative gains for these small auxiliary grids. Crucially, these optimizations leave the sampled estimator unchanged; the improvements arise from cheaper decisions rather than a different probability law.

8

Engineering ablation on four scenes at $\rho=0.98$ : (a) CPU time relative to full WiE, and (b) full spline evaluations per root sample with and without lazy squeeze. Each configuration uses identical seeds and $512$ samples per query.Figure 8.

General offspring distributions.

To validate the polynomial PGF formulation beyond binary branching, we evaluate an independent general-offspring WoS implementation with certified local $3\times 3$ B-spline envelopes on five two-dimensional problems, including pure quartic, mixed, and zero-offspring reactions (Table ). WiE improves time–variance efficiency across these cases, although the benefit depends strongly on geometry, boundary values, and the attainable envelope width. The table provides a generality test rather than a controlled comparison of offspring degree: reaction rates and domains vary between cases.

5

General PGF validation with $700$ samples per query. RMSE is measured against independent reference fields. Speedup is the BBM/WiE time–variance cost ratio (excluding local envelope construction). The local-spline experiment uses a separate general-PGF solver without multi-round refinement.Table 5.

Full-tree criticality in a ball.

Figure  illustrates the first-moment change for binary branching in the three-dimensional unit ball, with $g\equiv 0.75$ and the constant envelope $[0,0.75]$ .

9

The full-tree critical rate moves from $\lambda_{1}$ to $2\lambda_{1}$ . Left: the complete unit ball, a central section, and its center query. Right: exact expected reproduction counts, with $\rho=\lambda/\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{1}=\pi^{2}/2$ . BBM gives $k/\sin k-1$ , $k=\pi\sqrt{\rho}$ ; WiE gives $1.5(k_{w}/\sin k_{w}-1)$ , $k_{w}=\pi\sqrt{\rho/2}$ . Each expression is plotted only below its own critical rate.Figure 9. A complete translucent unit ball and analytical expected branching counts for BBM and constant-envelope WiE.

Radial validation.

Figure  compares WiE with an independent radial boundary-value solve on the three-dimensional unit ball.

10

Radial validation at $\lambda=2.1\lambda_{1}$ with boundary value $0.75$ . The full sphere encloses a reference section and seven query locations. The upper plot compares WiE with an independent radial BVP; the lower plot resolves the signed estimation error. Points pool three seeds of 8,192 samples; bars show 95% Monte Carlo confidence intervals. This test uses certified radial envelopes.Figure 10. A full sphere with seven radial queries beside the solution profile and signed estimation errors with confidence intervals.

Additional three-dimensional tests.

The following mesh tests solve $\frac{1}{2}\Delta u+\lambda(u^{2}-u)=0$ in the volumes enclosed by Fandisk, Bunny, Spot, and Rocker-arm , with $g(x)=h(x)=0.9-0.7(z_{\max}-z)/(z_{\max}-z_{\min})$ , analytic affine envelopes $(\ell,a)=(0,h)$ , $\lambda=2.1\widehat{\lambda}_{1}$ , and boundary tolerance $10^{-6}$ .

Here $\widehat{\lambda}_{1}$ is a finite-difference spectral estimate; these tests use the affine certificate without spline optimization or the preprocessing fallback.

The reference grids are $128^{3}$ for Fandisk, Bunny, and Spot, and $256^{3}$ for Rocker-arm; the last refinement changes the 48 held-out query values by RMS 0.00036, 0.00021, 0.00037, and 0.00045, respectively.

For the measured error–time comparisons, BBM samples boundary payoffs as Bernoulli outcomes and both implementations stop a root once a zero factor is known; these measurements do not evaluate full-tree work.

Figure  uses one pinned core of an Intel Xeon Silver 4310; total wall time includes mesh and BVH setup and sampling, plus analytic-envelope construction for WiE, while query generation, reference solves, rendering, and spectral analysis are excluded for both methods.(; ; ; )

Jacobson,

Stanford Computer Graphics Laboratory,

Sawhney, 2021

Crane et al., 2013

11

Error versus computation time at $\lambda=2.1\widehat{\lambda}_{1}$ . Each curve joins eight sample budgets $N=2^{6},\ldots,2^{13}$ ; each point averages the MSE of three independent seeds over 48 held-out volume queries. Time includes mesh setup and WiE envelope construction. Both implementations use early exit.Figure 11. Four measured time versus mean squared error plots for Fandisk, Bunny, Spot, and Rocker-arm.

Envelope quality and evaluation cost.

We further compare analytic affine envelopes with the final output of monotone B-spline construction on six meshes (Table ), using the same PDE, height-dependent boundary data, $\lambda=2.1\widehat{\lambda}_{1}$ , and boundary tolerance as above. The affine pair is $(\ell,a)=(0,h)$ . Cubic tensor-product splines use $9^{3}$ coefficients per envelope, start from $(0,0.9)$ , and allow up to eight refinement rounds, with a 60-second limit per LP. The 2,048 training points are independent of the 48 evaluation queries. Both representations use the same product estimator and exact termination after a zero factor.

6

At fixed $N=1{,}024$ , the five valid final spline configurations reduce the measured single-sample variance by $5.4$ – $21.0\%$ , but require $1.63$ – $4.05\times$ the sampling CPU time of the affine baseline, even before construction costs. Representing the identical affine envelopes as splines also increases sampling time by $1.17$ – $1.57\times$ , isolating representation and evaluation overhead. Fandisk and Spot accept no refinement and retain the initial envelope; the final Armadillo configuration requires event-probability repairs and is excluded from valid performance comparisons.

These results distinguish the variance bound from realized efficiency. The final spline envelopes have larger mean widths than the affine baseline; on Bunny, for example, the means are $0.582$ and $0.494$ , respectively, despite the lower measured spline variance. Equation () remains a valid worst-case bound, but when attainable envelopes remain broad, it can provide limited guidance for predicting actual variance or selecting the fastest representation. Lower measured variance alone is also insufficient: its benefit must offset the cost of sampling and envelope construction. For these tests, inexpensive analytic affine envelopes offer the better computational tradeoff while retaining WiE’s envelope transformation.

4

Envelope comparison at a fixed sample budget. $V$ is the mean single-sample variance over 48 queries and eight independent runs; $t$ is the mean sampling CPU time in seconds for all 48 queries, with $N=1{,}024$ samples per query. Construction is excluded. A: analytic affine; S: final spline-construction output. $\dagger$ : no accepted update, so S is the initial $(0,0.9)$ envelope. Dashes denote the failed Armadillo sampling audit.Table 6.

Interior field visualizations.

Figure  shows the complete Spot model and a translucent plane locating its $z=0$ query section. An independent 16-sample pilot fixes the sample count for a nominal 60-second total budget; reported times include the pilot and analytic-envelope construction. The raw field panels share query locations and color scales, without smoothing or denoising.

12

Spot at $\lambda=2.1\widehat{\lambda}_{1}$ . The full mesh and translucent blue plane locate the $z=0$ section; the flat panels show the independent $128^{3}$ reference and raw BBM/WiE estimates on identical queries. Times include the pilot and envelope construction; RMSE covers the entire section. The flat field panels use one unlit color scale.Figure 12. Complete Spot mesh with a translucent evaluation plane and three corresponding unlit solution fields.

Figure  applies the same field-visualization protocol to Rocker-arm.

13

Rocker-arm at $\lambda=2.1\widehat{\lambda}_{1}$ . The full mesh and translucent blue plane locate the $z=0$ section; the flat panels show the independent $256^{3}$ reference and raw BBM/WiE estimates on identical queries. Times include the pilot and envelope construction; RMSE covers the entire section. The flat field panels use one unlit color scale.Figure 13. Complete Rocker-arm mesh with a translucent evaluation plane and three corresponding unlit solution fields.

6.

WiE demonstrates that certified solution bounds can reshape branching dynamics rather than merely prune existing trees. While the transformation preserves unbiasedness, its efficiency depends on envelope quality and sampling acceptance rates. Constructing certified envelopes incurs preprocessing costs, making WiE less advantageous for low branching intensities or limited query workloads. Our spectral-workload fallback mitigates this overhead but relies on empirical calibration. Moreover, the near-critical complexity guarantee bounds expected reproduction events rather than total runtime. Extensions to manifold and parabolic PDEs demonstrate broader applicability, although projected walks inherit geometric approximation errors and space-time sampling introduces additional costs. Future work may include higher-dimensional certification and more efficient envelope optimization directly targeting computational work.

item.content:encoded:
一句话：不去剪枝已有树，而是直接改造分支扩散过程，在临界分支率附近大幅降本且保持无偏。

要点：

  • 分支 Walk-on-Spheres 无需网格即可求解半线性 PDE，但分支率接近临界值时成本爆炸
  • 利用可认证的解界抑制繁殖，并引入可控终止
  • 在保持估计无偏的前提下显著降低成本

为什么值得看：体积渲染、参与介质、PDE 求解都用得到蒙特卡洛游走；这套「改造过程而非剪枝」的思路可以迁移到任何分支型采样器。

中文摘要：分支式球面游走（Branching Walk-on-Spheres）可以在无网格条件下求解半线性 PDE，但当分支率接近临界值时计算成本急剧增长。作者提出 Walk in Envelopes：利用可认证的解界来变换分支扩散过程本身，而不是事后剪枝已有树——通过抑制繁殖、引入受控终止，在保持无偏性的同时显著降低成本。这类方法可直接用于参与介质渲染与相关模拟。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

Walk in Envelopes: Efficient Branching Walk-on-Spheres via Certified Solution Bounds

Yunfeng Liao

, , , Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)ShenzhenGuangdongChina, Zhenhao Qiu

, , , Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)ShenzhenGuangdongChina, Xinyang Chen

, , , Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)ShenzhenGuangdongChina and Xiucheng Li

, , , Affiliation: Harbin Institute of Technology (Shenzhen)ShenzhenGuangdongChina© none

Walk in Envelopes (WiE) transforms branching WoS using certified lower and upper solution bounds. By reparameterizing the solution within a spatially varying envelope, WiE redistributes the original branching mechanism into splitting, return-0, and return-1 events, enabling early termination and pruning of redundant branches while preserving the target solution. The resulting computation trees are substantially smaller than those of conventional branching WoS.Figure 1. 1

Abstract.

Branching Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) solves semilinear PDEs without meshes, but its computational cost grows sharply near critical branching rates. We introduce (WiE), which uses certified solution bounds to transform branching diffusion rather than prune existing trees. The transformation suppresses reproduction, introduces controlled termination, and preserves unbiasedness with an envelope-dependent variance bound. We realize the transformed process through exact rejection sampling using standard screened WoS kernels, supported by certified spline envelopes and adaptive sampling and further prove that suitable harmonic envelopes yield bounded expected reproduction counts even as conventional BBM diverges.Walk in Envelopes

Walk-on-Spheres, Branching Brownian Motion, Semilinear PDEs, Certified Solution Bounds, Monte Carlo Methods

Keywords:

1.

Grid-free Monte Carlo methods have become an attractive alternative to mesh-based PDE solvers, enabling pointwise solution queries on complex domains without constructing a global discretization . While Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) efficiently resolves linear elliptic equations through boundary-hitting processes, extending this paradigm to semilinear PDEs requires handling nonlinear reactions. Branching Brownian motion (BBM) provides a natural probabilistic representation by replacing nonlinear terms with particle reproduction events . Combined with WoS, this yields a grid-free solver for semilinear equations. However, eliminating Brownian time discretization does not eliminate branching complexity: each offspring initiates additional walks, and the expected particle population diverges as the branching intensity approaches a critical spectral threshold. This makes otherwise valid stochastic representations increasingly expensive precisely in strongly nonlinear regimes.()

Sawhney and Crane, 2020

()

Agarwal and Claisse, 2020

A natural strategy is to exploit approximate solution information to terminate branches whose remaining contributions are sufficiently small. Yet such pruning requires reliable bounds on unresolved subtrees, whose evaluation can itself be expensive. Approximate bounds may also introduce bias, while tighter estimates do not necessarily offset their computation costs. More fundamentally, pruning acts on a branching process that has already been generated, rather than preventing unnecessary reproduction. This motivates a different question: can certified solution information be used to construct an equivalent stochastic process that branches less frequently, without sacrificing correctness?

We introduce (WiE), a branching WoS framework that transforms the stochastic representation using certified lower and upper solution envelopes. Given sub- and supersolutions $\ell\leq u\leq a$ , we normalize the unknown solution as $v=(u-\ell)/(a-\ell)$ . This induces a generalized Doob transform whose diffusion, reproduction, and termination mechanisms are determined by the envelope functions. For binary branching, the reproduction rate becomes $\lambda(a-\ell)$ , while envelope residuals introduce additional success and failure termination events. The resulting estimator remains unbiased and has variance bounded by $(a-\ell)^{2}/4$ . Moreover, we characterize its expected reproduction count through an elliptic equation, showing that a suitable harmonic envelope can keep this count uniformly bounded even as conventional BBM approaches its critical divergence threshold. Although branching-process transformations have established mathematical foundations , WiE develops them into a certified computational framework for semilinear PDE solving.Walk in Envelopes()

Engländer, 2007

The transformed process introduces spatially varying diffusion, which would ordinarily require simulating drifted trajectories. We avoid this difficulty by deriving an exact envelope-aware transition using the original screened WoS exit and Green kernels. Rejection sampling with certified local majorants realizes the transformed distribution without evaluating weighted kernel integrals. To obtain useful envelopes efficiently, we develop monotone refinement of cubic B-spline sub- and supersolutions, using Bernstein constraints to certify PDE inequalities throughout the domain by comparison principle. Adaptive screening, spatially localized rejection bounds, and lazy evaluation further reduce sampling overhead, while a spectral-workload criterion avoids unnecessary preprocessing in inexpensive regimes.

We evaluate WiE on four complex two-dimensional domains across branching intensities and accuracy requirements. Near criticality, WiE achieves $6.9$ – $16.2\times$ improvements in time–variance efficiency and $4.7$ – $14.6\times$ reductions in sampling time at matched accuracy, excluding one-time envelope construction. Its benefits increase with branching intensity, while a workload-aware fallback preserves the efficiency of conventional BBM in easier regimes. We additionally demonstrate extensions to projected walks on manifolds and semilinear parabolic equations.

Our main contributions are:

•

A certified envelope transformation of branching diffusion, with unbiased estimation, variance guarantees, and a spectral characterization of near-critical branching complexity.

•

An exact envelope-aware WoS sampler using existing screened kernels, without explicitly simulating transformed diffusion.

•

A practical solver combining certified spline-envelope refinement, efficient rejection sampling, and workload-aware fallback, with substantial near-critical acceleration.

2.

Branching Diffusions and Solution-Guided Transformations.

BBM represents semilinear reaction–diffusion PDEs, beginning with McKean’s Kolmogorov–Petrovskii–Piskunov representation . Branching-diffusion solvers extend to polynomial nonlinearities, gradient dependence via marked particles , and elliptic boundary-value problems on bounded domains , but face integrability and branching-cost restrictions under strong branching. Process transformations are well established: nonlinear $h$ -transforms alter both motion and reproduction , while measure changes and backbone decompositions characterize conditioned branching and near-critical behavior . These underpin solution-guided representations. Our computational realization uses certified sub- and supersolutions to obtain nonnegative branching and killing rates, with exact sphere-transition sampling requiring neither the unknown solution nor drifted-trajectory simulation.()

Monte Carlo Methods for Nonlinear Equations.

Monte Carlo solvers avoid global spatial discretization, but nested nonlinear expectations and recursive branching can sharply increase variance and work. Numerical branching methods handle polynomial nonlinear PDEs, subject to representation-dependent convergence and integrability . In graphics, accelerate nonlinear recursive light transport through nonlinear path filtering that reuses intermediate evaluations and neural radiance caching that learns them. For nonlinear radiative boundary conditions, combine Picard-style iteration with Monte Carlo PDE solvers. These reduce nonlinear integral-equation costs through reuse, approximation, or iteration. Instead, we retain a branching estimator but change its probability law: certified envelopes suppress reproduction, bound its range, and preserve its expectation under stated assumptions. We reduce sample-generation work rather than only accelerate or approximate an existing recursion.(; )

Walk-on-Spheres and Grid-Free PDE Solvers.

WoS originated for Dirichlet problems and entered geometric computing as a grid-free elliptic PDE solver for point queries . Extensions handle spatially varying coefficients via null scattering , mixed Neumann–Dirichlet conditions via walk on stars , and boundary-integral transport via walk on boundary . Boundary-value caching reuses estimates across queries , differential WoS computes parameter derivatives , and projected walks solve surface PDEs . These advances mainly address linear PDE representations, boundary handling, or stochastic-estimate reuse. For semilinear PDEs, sphere jumps eliminate Brownian time discretization but not branching-tree growth. We target this remaining bottleneck through certified semilinear bounds and a transformed process with weighted exit and interior events sampled using the original screened WoS kernels.()

3.1.

Branching Brownian motion (BBM) provides a stochastic representation of semilinear elliptic PDEs by interpreting nonlinear reactions as particle branching events. Consider $F(u):=\mathcal{L}u+\lambda(P(u)-u)=0$ with Dirichlet condition $u|_{\partial\Omega}=g$ , where $P(u)=\sum_{k=0}^{K}p_{k}u^{k}$ is the offspring generating function and $\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{2}\Delta$ . Each particle follows Brownian motion until either reaching the boundary or branching into $k$ independent offspring with probability $p_{k}$ at an exponential rate $\lambda$ . The solution is recovered as $u(x)=\mathbb{E}[\prod_{i\in\mathcal{T}}g(X_{i})]$ , where $\mathcal{T}$ is the terminal leaves.

For probabilistic semilinear elliptic PDEs, Dirichlet values naturally lie in $[0,1]$ . For example, $g(y)\in[0,1]$ may specify the success probability of a particle absorbed at $y$ , in which case $u(x)$ gives the probability that every terminal particle succeeds. This interpretation follows directly from the BBM representation $u(x)=\mathbb{E}[\prod_{i\in\mathcal{L}}g(X_{i})]$ , and ensures $0\leq u\leq 1$ .

Branching WoS accelerates this process by replacing Brownian trajectories with sphere transitions. At each particle position $x$ , let $B=B(x,r)\subset\Omega$ be the largest inscribed ball, and denote by $H_{\lambda}$ and $G_{\lambda}$ its screened exit and Green kernels, respectively. Conditioning on whether the particle exits the ball before branching yields the integral equation induced by total expectation:

(1) $u(x)=\int_{\partial B}H_{\lambda}(x,\mathrm{d}y)\,u(y)+\lambda\int_{B}G_{\lambda}(x,y)\sum_{k=0}^{K}p_{k}u(y)^{k}\,\mathrm{d}y.$

Specifically, the exit probability is $q_{B}=\int_{\partial B}H_{\lambda}(x,\mathrm{d}y)=1/I_{0}(r\sqrt{2\lambda})$ in $\mathbb{R}^{2}$ , where $I_{0}$ denotes the modified Bessel function. With probability $q_{B}$ , the particle jumps uniformly to $\partial B$ and continues walking; otherwise, an interior branching location $Y$ is sampled with density $\lambda G_{\lambda}(x,y)/(1-q_{B})$ , and $k\sim(p_{k})$ offspring are added to the active particle queue at $Y$ . The procedure repeats until all particles reach the domain boundary or terminate with zero offspring, producing one Monte Carlo sample from the product of terminal values. Thus, although WoS eliminates explicit trajectory discretization, each sphere transition still requires a branching decision, while every offspring introduces additional walks that must be maintained and evaluated. Canonical results show that BWoS crashes when the particle splitting rate surpasses the boundary-absorbing speed, i.e., $\lambda>\lambda_{1}$ where $\lambda_{1}$ is the least non-negative eigenvalue of $-\mathcal{L}$ in $\Omega$ .

3.2.

Although WoS eliminates explicit Brownian trajectory discretization, its computational cost still grows with the branching tree. The expected cumulative particle population becomes unbounded as $\lambda$ approaches the principal Dirichlet eigenvalue $\lambda_{1}$ associated with $\Omega$ , motivating the early termination of subtrees whose remaining contributions can be bounded. Let $\tau$ denote the first Brownian exit time from $\Omega$ , and $h(x)=\mathbb{E}_{x}[g(B_{\tau})]$ the harmonic extension of $g$ . Several bounds follow directly from the BBM representation and its associated linear equations as Theorem .

3.1

Theorem 3.1 (Probabilistic Solution Bounds).

For $0<\lambda<\lambda_{1},P(u)=u^{2}$ and $0\leq g\leq 1$ , the solution of $F(u)=0$ with $u|{\partial\Omega}=g$ satisfies ${\max}\{L_{0}(x),L_{1}(x),L_{2}(x)\}\leq u(x)\leq U(x),$

where $U=h$ , and $L_{0}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{x}[e^{-\lambda\tau}g(B\tau)]$ , $L_{1}(x)=1-\mathbb{E}_{x}[e^{\lambda\tau}(1-g(B_{\tau}))]$ , $L_{2}(x)=h(x)-\tfrac{\lambda}{4}\mathbb{E}_{x}[\tau]$ .

Proof.

Since $F(u)=0$ implies $\mathcal{L}u=\lambda u(1-u)\geq 0$ , the maximum principle gives $u\leq h=U$ . For $L_{0}$ , restrict the BBM expectation to trajectories reaching the boundary before their first branching event; all omitted products are nonnegative, yielding $u\geq\mathbb{E}_{x}[e^{-\lambda\tau}g(B_{\tau})]$ . For $L_{1}$ , let $q=1-u$ . Then $\mathcal{L}q+\lambda q=\lambda q^{2}\geq 0$ . The Feynman–Kac formula gives $q(x)=\mathbb{E}_{x}[e^{\lambda\tau}(1-g(B_{\tau}))]-\lambda\mathbb{E}_{x}[\int_{0}^{\tau}e^{\lambda t}q(B_{t})^{2}\,\mathrm{d}t]$ , hence $u\geq L_{1}$ . Finally, Dynkin’s formula gives $h-u=\lambda\mathbb{E}_{x}[\int_{0}^{\tau}u(B_{t})(1-u(B_{t}))\,\mathrm{d}t]$ . Since $u(1-u)\leq 1/4$ , we obtain $u\geq L_{2}$ .

∎

These bounds enable early termination of unresolved branching subtrees. Suppose the completed leaves contribute a product $\omega\in[0,1]$ , while the active frontier contains particles at $x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}$ . By conditional independence, their remaining expected contribution is $R=\omega\prod_{i=1}^{m}u(x_{i})$ . With bounds $L\leq u\leq U$ immediately yield

(2) $B^{-}:=\omega\prod_{i=1}^{m}L(x_{i})\leq R\leq\omega\prod_{i=1}^{m}U(x_{i}):=B^{+}.$

Thus, whenever $B^{+}-B^{-}\leq 2\varepsilon$ , the remaining tree can be pruned and replaced by $(B^{-}+B^{+})/2$ , introducing at most $\varepsilon$ absolute bias in the final expectation, since the conditional expected contribution lies within $[B^{-},B^{+}]$ .

Pruning speedup relative to vanilla WoS–BBM (dashed $1\times$ ) across branching rates $\beta$ , for constant, $P_{2}$ , $P_{10}$ , and binary-hemisphere boundary data (mean $0.5$ ).Figure 2.

Despite their validity, these bounds incur evaluation overhead and exhibit strongly case-dependent efficiency (Fig. ). $L_{0}$ ignores branched trajectories, $L_{1}$ deteriorates with large boundary deficits, while $L_{2}$ relies on the worst-case bound $u(1-u)\leq 1/4$ . Consequently, $L_{2}$ generally performs best on smooth boundaries, whereas discontinuous binary data defeats most pruning with binary boundary condition. Combining all bounds often increases overhead without proportional savings. This motivates certified envelopes that directly reduce branching rather than repeatedly pruning existing trees.

3.3.

The preceding pruning strategy uses solution bounds to terminate subtrees after they have been generated, but does not alter the underlying branching dynamics. We instead construct an equivalent branching process whose reproduction and termination rates are determined directly by certified solution envelopes. This can be understood as a generalized Doob’s $h$ -transform, where the envelope width acts as the transforming function.

For $F(u)=0$ , let $\ell$ and $a$ be certified sub- and supersolutions satisfying $0\leq\ell\leq u\leq a\leq 1$ , $F(\ell)\geq 0$ , and $F(a)\leq 0$ . Define the domain envelop width $d:=a-\ell>0$ , the normalized solution $v=(u-\ell)/d\in[0,1]$ , and the nonnegative residuals $r_{\ell}=F(\ell)$ and $r_{a}=-F(a)$ . By substituting $u=\ell+dv$ and expanding the offspring generating function, we obtain

$P(\ell+dv)=P(\ell)+\sum_{j=1}^{K}C_{j}v^{j},\qquad C_{j}=\frac{P^{(j)}(\ell)}{j!}d^{j}\geq 0.$

The key is that the transformation changes not only the diffusion operator but also the branching mechanism into four parts – drifted diffusion $\mathcal{L}^{d}v$ , reduced branching $\sum_{j=2}^{K}{\lambda C_{j}(v^{j}-v)}/{d}$ , returning one $r_{c}(1-v)/d$ and zero (being killed) $-{r_{a}}v/{d}$ in the theorem below.

Theorem 3.2 (Generalized Envelope Branching).

With certified envelopes satisfying the conditions above and well-defined and integrable transformed branching process, $v=(u-\ell)/d$ satisfies

(3) $\displaystyle 0=\mathcal{L}^{d}v+\sum_{j=2}^{K}\frac{\lambda C_{j}}{d}(v^{j}-v)+\frac{r_{\ell}}{d}(1-v)-\frac{r_{a}}{d}v,$

where $\mathcal{L}^{d}=\mathcal{L}+\nabla\log d\cdot\nabla$ . Consequently, the equivalent process branches into $j\geq 2$ offspring at rate $\lambda C_{j}/d$ , terminates successfully at rate $r_{\ell}/d$ , and terminates unsuccessfully at rate $r_{a}/d$ . If $W\in[0,1]$ is its terminal-product estimator, then $Z(x)=\ell(x)+d(x)W$ is unbiased $\mathbb{E}[Z(x)]=u(x)$ and

(4) $\operatorname{Var}[Z(x)]\leq(u(x)-\ell(x))(a(x)-u(x))\leq{d(x)^{2}}/{4}.$

Proof.

The product rule gives $\mathcal{L}(dv)=d\mathcal{L}^{d}v+v\mathcal{L}d$ , where $\mathcal{L}^{d}v=d^{-1}[\mathcal{L}(dv)-v\mathcal{L}d]$ . Since $F(a)-F(\ell)=-r_{a}-r_{\ell}$ and $P(a)-P(\ell)=\sum_{j=1}^{K}C_{j}$ , we have $\mathcal{L}d-\lambda d=-r_{\ell}-r_{a}-\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{K}C_{j}$ . Substituting these identities into $F(\ell+dv)=0$ yields $d\mathcal{L}^{d}v+r_{\ell}(1-v)-r_{a}v+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{K}C_{j}(v^{j}-v)=0$ . The $j=1$ term vanishes, giving Eq. (). Its nonnegative rates define the stated branching process, with boundary payoff $(g-\ell)/d\in[0,1]$ . The branching representation gives $\mathbb{E}[W]=v$ , hence $\mathbb{E}[Z]=u$ . Finally, $Z\in[\ell,a]$ implies $\mathbb{E}[(Z-\ell)(a-Z)]\geq 0$ , which yields Eq. ().

Beyond preserving the original PDE solution, it also changes the expected branching complexity. For conventional BBM, the expected number of reproduction events $m_{B}$ satisfies

$(-\mathcal{L}-\lambda)m_{B}=\lambda$ , with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. The transformed process instead obeys the following equation.

Lemma 3.3 (Expected Branching Complexity).

Let $m_{\ell,a}(x)$ denote the expected number of reproduction events in the transformed process, assumed finite. Then $H=m_{\ell,a}d$ satisfies $H|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ and

(5) $\left[-\mathcal{L}+\lambda(1-P^{\prime}(a))\right]H=\lambda[P(a)-P(\ell)-P^{\prime}(\ell)d].$

Proof.

Writing $b_{j}=\lambda C_{j}/d$ and

$\kappa=(r_{\ell}+r_{a})/d$ , the first-event decomposition gives

(6) $-\mathcal{L}^{d}m_{\ell,a}+\left[\kappa-\sum_{j=2}^{K}(j-1)b_{j}\right]m_{\ell,a}=\sum_{j=2}^{K}b_{j}.$

Multiplying by $d$ and using

$\mathcal{L}d=\lambda d-r_{\ell}-r_{a}-\lambda\sum_{j=1}^{K}C_{j}$ ,

together with

$\sum_{j=1}^{K}jC_{j}=P^{\prime}(a)d$ and

$\sum_{j=2}^{K}C_{j}=P(a)-P(\ell)-P^{\prime}(\ell)d$ ,

yields the stated equation.

∎

For binary branching, this reduces to $\left[-\mathcal{L}+\lambda(1-2a)\right]H=\lambda d^{2}.$ Thus, the transformation changes both the source of branching work and the elliptic operator governing its propagation. In particular, narrowing the envelope suppresses the quadratic source term, while the upper envelope controls the effective reproduction potential. These effects explain how WiE can reduce branching complexity even when conventional BBM approaches its critical regime. Also, there exists a harmonic envelope such that the cost of WiE keeps finite as the splitting rate approaches the divergence limit of vanilla WoS in theory as Theorem  reveals.

Theorem 3.4 (Bounded near-critical branching with harmonic envelopes).

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be a bounded, connected $C^{2,\alpha}$ domain, and let $\lambda_{1}>0$ be the principal Dirichlet eigenvalue of $-\mathcal{L}$ , where $\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{2}\Delta$ . Suppose $g\in C^{2,\alpha}(\partial\Omega)$ satisfies $0\leq g\leq 1$ , $g\not\equiv 0$ , and $g\not\equiv 1$ . Let $h$ be its harmonic extension, $\mathcal{L}h=0$ in $\Omega$ and $h=g$ on $\partial\Omega$ . For the binary branching equation $\mathcal{L}u+\lambda(u^{2}-u)=0$ , choose the certified envelopes $\ell=0$ and $a=h$ . Then the expected reproduction count $m_{\lambda}$ of the transformed process satisfies

(7) $\sup_{0<\lambda<\lambda_{1}}|m_{\lambda}|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}<\infty.$

In contrast, the expected reproduction count $m_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{BBM}}$ of conventional binary BBM diverges as $\lambda\uparrow\lambda_{1}$ : for every fixed $x\in\Omega$ , $m_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{BBM}}(x)=\Theta((\lambda_{1}-\lambda)^{-1})$ .

Proof.

The strong maximum principle gives $00$ in the interior. By Lemma 3.3, $H_{\lambda}:=hm_{\lambda}$ solves

(8) $A_{\lambda}H_{\lambda}=\lambda h^{2},\qquad H_{\lambda}|{\partial\Omega}=0,\qquad A\lambda=-\mathcal{L}-\lambda+2\lambda(1-h).$

We first show that $A_{\lambda}$ has a spectral gap uniform up to $\lambda_{1}$ . At $\lambda=\lambda_{1}$ , its quadratic form is

(9) $\langle f,A_{\lambda_{1}}f\rangle=\underbrace{\|\nabla f\|_{2}^{2}/2-\lambda_{1}\|f\|_{2}^{2}}_{\geq 0}+2\lambda_{1}\int_{\Omega}(1-h)f^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x.$

If its lowest eigenvalue were zero, equality would force $f$ to be a multiple of the positive first Dirichlet eigenfunction $\phi_{1}$ and simultaneously $\int_{\Omega}(1-h)f^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x=0$ , contradicting $1-h>0$ in $\Omega$ . Hence $\kappa:=\lambda_{\min}(A_{\lambda_{1}})>0$ . Writing $t=\lambda/\lambda_{1}$ gives $A_{\lambda}=(1-t)(-\mathcal{L})+tA_{\lambda_{1}}$ , so the min–max principle yields

(10) $\lambda_{\min}(A_{\lambda})\geq(1-t)\lambda_{1}+t\kappa\geq\min{\lambda_{1},\kappa}>0.$

Uniform invertibility and standard Dirichlet elliptic estimates therefore imply $|H_{\lambda}|{C^{1}(\overline{\Omega})}\leq C$ , with $C$ independent of $\lambda\in(0,\lambda_{1})$ . Since $H\lambda=0$ on $\partial\Omega$ , $|H_{\lambda}(x)|\leq C,\mathrm{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)$ . On the other hand, positivity of $h$ in the interior, the Hopf boundary lemma at points where $g=0$ , and compactness of $\partial\Omega$ imply $h(x)\geq c,\mathrm{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)$ for some $c>0$ . Thus $m_{\lambda}=H_{\lambda}/h\leq C/c$ throughout $\Omega$ , proving the bound.

For conventional BBM, $(-\mathcal{L}-\lambda)m_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{BBM}}=\lambda$ with zero Dirichlet boundary data. The isolated principal-eigenvalue resolvent expansion gives

(11) $m_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{BBM}}(x)=\frac{\lambda_{1}\langle 1,\phi_{1}\rangle\phi_{1}(x)}{\lambda_{1}-\lambda}+O_{x}(1),\qquad\lambda\uparrow\lambda_{1},$

where $|\phi_{1}|_{2}=1$ . This proves the stated divergence.
