12

The remaining challenge is sampling this distribution without evaluating its weighted integrals. Although Eq. () provides the normalizing constant $d(x)$ , directly sampling a density proportional to $H_{\lambda}d$ or $G_{\lambda}\omega_{I}$ would require a new sampler for each spatially varying envelope. Instead, we use rejection sampling to recover these densities from the original WoS proposals.

14

Specifically, the target exit and interior transition measures are proportional to $H_{\lambda}(x,\mathrm{d}y)d(y)$ and $\lambda G_{\lambda}(x,y)\omega_{I}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y$ , respectively. We therefore introduce two certified constants $M_{E}\geq\sup_{\partial B}d$ and $M_{I}\geq\sup_{B}\omega_{I}$ to dominate these weighted measures by distributions that are already straightforward to sample. Let $q_{B}=\int_{\partial B}H_{\lambda}(x,\mathrm{d}y)$ denote the original sphere-exit probability. The corresponding proposal masses are $q_{B}M_{E}$ for exits and $(1-q_{B})M_{I}$ for interior events, giving the computable normalization $Q_{B}=q_{B}M_{E}+(1-q_{B})M_{I}$ .

We first choose an exit proposal with probability $q_{B}M_{E}/Q_{B}$ , otherwise an interior proposal. Its position $Y$ is drawn from $H_{\lambda}/q_{B}$ or $\lambda G_{\lambda}/(1-q_{B})$ , respectively, and accepted with probability $d(Y)/M_{E}$ or $\omega_{I}(Y)/M_{I}$ . For example, the joint probability measure of proposing and accepting an exit at $y$ is $\frac{q_{B}M_{E}}{Q_{B}}\frac{H_{\lambda}(x,\mathrm{d}y)}{q_{B}}\frac{d(y)}{M_{E}}=\frac{H_{\lambda}(x,\mathrm{d}y)d(y)}{Q_{B}}.$

Similarly, the accepted interior measure is $\lambda G_{\lambda}(x,y)\omega_{I}(y)\,\mathrm{d}y/Q_{B}$ . Their total mass is $d(x)/Q_{B}$ by Eq. (). Conditioning on acceptance therefore divides both measures by $d(x)/Q_{B}$ , recovering exactly the target transition probabilities. Thus, the accpetance rate is $d(x)/Q_{B}$ and rejected candidates can simply be resampled. Notice that neither the target normalization $d(x)$ nor any weighted Green integral needs to be evaluated during sampling.

4.1.

The transformation admits many certified envelopes with different computational costs. We construct tight, reusable bounds for full-field evaluation through four steps: a comparison principle certifies bounds from PDE residuals and boundary conditions; query-weighted envelope width approximates the intractable time–variance objective; conservative affine constraints monotonically refine an initially feasible pair; and cubic B-splines with cellwise Bernstein constraints reduce continuous certification to finite-dimensional linear programs. Certification is preserved throughout, while preprocessing is amortized across repeated queries.

Lemma 4.1 (Comparison Principle for Certified Envelopes).

For a bounded Lipschitz domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , assume $\lambda\geq 0$ and $\lambda\sup_{s\in[0,1]}\allowbreak(P^{\prime}(s)-1)<\lambda_{1}.$ Suppose $u,\ell,a\in C^{2}(\Omega)\cap C(\overline{\Omega})\cap H^{1}(\Omega)$ take values in $[0,1]$ and satisfy $F(u)=0,F(\ell)\geq 0,F(a)\leq 0$ and

$\ell\leq u\leq a$ on $\partial\Omega$ . Then

$\ell\leq u\leq a$ throughout $\Omega$ .

Proof.

We first prove $\ell\leq u$ . Set $w=\ell-u$ . Since

$F(\ell)-F(u)\geq 0$ , subtracting the two PDE residuals gives $\mathcal{L}w+\lambda\bigl(P(\ell)-P(u)-w\bigr)\geq 0.$ To rewrite the nonlinear difference as a term proportional to $w$ ,

apply the fundamental theorem of calculus pointwise:

(18) $P(\ell(x))-P(u(x))=\int_{u(x)}^{\ell(x)}P^{\prime}(s)\,\mathrm{d}s=w(x)\int_{0}^{1}P^{\prime}\bigl(u(x)+tw(x)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t.$

Define the bounded coefficient $q(x)=\int_{0}^{1}P^{\prime}\bigl(u(x)+tw(x)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t.$ Because $0\leq u,\ell\leq 1$ , every argument of $P^{\prime}$ lies in $[0,1]$ , and thus

(19) $\lambda(q(x)-1)\leq\lambda\sup_{s\in[0,1]}(P^{\prime}(s)-1)<\lambda_{1}.$

It follows that $\frac{1}{2}\Delta w+\lambda(q(x)-1)w\geq 0,\qquad w\leq 0\quad\text{on }\partial\Omega.$ We now justify the maximum-principle step rather than assuming it.

Let $w_{+}=\max\{w,0\}$ . Since $w\leq 0$ on the boundary and

$w\in H^{1}(\Omega)$ , we have $w_{+}\in H_{0}^{1}(\Omega)$ . Multiplying the

last differential inequality by $w_{+}$ and integrating by parts gives

(20) $0\leq-\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla w_{+}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x+\lambda\int_{\Omega}(q(x)-1)w_{+}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x.$

Consequently,

(21) $\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla w_{+}|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\leq c_{*}\int_{\Omega}w_{+}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x,\qquad c_{*}:=\lambda\sup_{s\in[0,1]}(P^{\prime}(s)-1).$

The variational characterization of the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of

$-\frac{1}{2}\Delta$ states that, for any $\varphi\in H_{0}^{1}(\Omega)$ , $\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla\varphi|^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\geq\lambda_{1}\int_{\Omega}\varphi^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x.$ Applying this inequality to $\varphi=w_{+}$ yields $(\lambda_{1}-c_{*})\int_{\Omega}w_{+}^{2}\,\mathrm{d}x\leq 0.$

Since $\lambda_{1}-c_{*}>0$ , we obtain $w_{+}=0$ , hence $\ell\leq u$ .

To prove $u\leq a$ , repeat the same argument with $w=u-a$ .

Indeed, $F(u)-F(a)\geq 0$ , $w\leq 0$ on the boundary, and $P(u)-P(a)=w\int_{0}^{1}P^{\prime}\bigl(a+t(u-a)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}t.$

The same upper bound on the resulting zero-order coefficient

and the same energy argument show $(u-a)_{+}=0$ . Thus

$\ell\leq u\leq a$ in $\Omega$ .

∎

Work-aware envelope optimization.

Let $\mathcal{Q}\subset\Omega$ denote the evaluation region and let $T_{\ell,a}(x)$ and $V_{\ell,a}(x)$ be the expected runtime and estimator variance induced by a certified envelope pair $(\ell,a)$ . For full-field evaluation, the ideal envelopes minimize the total cost of reaching a prescribed accuracy $\int_{\mathcal{Q}}T_{\ell,a}(x)V_{\ell,a}(x)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(x)$ . Here $\mu$ describes the distribution of evaluation queries. The objective reflects the time–variance cost of independent Monte Carlo evaluation, but is difficult to optimize directly because $T_{\ell,a}$ depends on the entire transformed branching process.

Fortunately, the envelope width $d=a-\ell$ provides a tractable surrogate. From Eq. (), the transformed reproduction coefficients are $C_{j}=P^{(j)}(\ell)d^{j}/j!$ . In particular, for binary branching, the probability mass associated with reproduction is proportional to $d^{2}$ . Moreover, Eq. () bounds the estimator variance by $d^{2}/4$ . These observations motivate minimizing the domain-averaged envelope width which replaces $T_{\ell,a}(x)V_{\ell,a}(x)$ , yielding

12

4

(22) $\displaystyle\min_{\ell,a}$ $\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{Q}}(a(x)-\ell(x))\,\mathrm{d}\mu(x),$ $\displaystyle\mathrm{s.t.}$ $\displaystyle F(\ell)\geq 0,F(a)\leq 0,0\leq\ell\leq a\leq 1,\ell|_{\partial\Omega}\leq g\leq a|_{\partial\Omega}.$

This objective seeks a single pair of reusable envelopes rather than independently optimizing bounds at each evaluation point. While width reduction does not guarantee a proportional runtime improvement, it simultaneously suppresses higher-order reproduction terms and tightens the estimator’s variance bound.

Starting from valid bounds $\ell(x)\leq u(x)\leq a(x)$ , nonnegative corrections $h_{t}$ and $j_{t}$ monotonically tighten the lower and upper envelopes while preserving feasibility. Bernstein coefficients provide finite-dimensional sufficient conditions for continuous certification.Figure 4.

Monotone certified refinement.

The optimization in Eq. () is nonlinear because the envelope constraints involve the reaction term $P$ . We therefore begin with a feasible pair $(\ell_{0},a_{0})$ and construct a sequence of increasingly tight certified envelopes. At iteration $t$ , we seek nonnegative corrections $h_{t},j_{t}$ such that

22

(23) $\ell_{t+1}=\ell_{t}+h_{t},\qquad a_{t+1}=a_{t}-j_{t}.$

The corresponding optimization maximizes the improvement

(24) $\displaystyle\max_{h_{t},j_{t}\geq 0}$ $\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{Q}}(h_{t}+j_{t})\,\mathrm{d}\mu,$ $\displaystyle\mathrm{s.t.}$ $\displaystyle F(\ell_{t}+h_{t})\geq 0,\quad F(a_{t}-j_{t})\leq 0,\quad\ell_{t}+h_{t}\leq a_{t}-j_{t},$

together with the original range and boundary constraints. Feasibility at every iteration implies

(25) $\ell_{t}\leq\ell_{t+1}\leq u\leq a_{t+1}\leq a_{t},\qquad\mathcal{J}(\ell_{t+1},a_{t+1})\leq\mathcal{J}(\ell_{t},a_{t}).$

Thus, refinement never sacrifices a previously certified bound, and every accepted update improves the surrogate objective (Figure ).

4

For a general offspring generating function $P(u)=\sum_{k=0}^{K}p_{k}u^{k}$ , the nonlinear certification constraints can be converted into affine sufficient conditions by exploiting the convexity of $P$ on $[0,1]$ . Substituting the monotone updates yields

(26) $\displaystyle F(\ell_{t}+h_{t})$ $\displaystyle=F(\ell_{t})+[\mathcal{L}+\lambda(P^{\prime}(\ell_{t})-1)]h_{t}+\lambda R_{\ell}(h_{t}),$ $\displaystyle-F(a_{t}-j_{t})$ $\displaystyle=-F(a_{t})+[\mathcal{L}+\lambda(P^{\prime}(a_{t})-1)]j_{t}-\lambda R_{a}(j_{t}),$

where the Taylor remainders satisfy

(27) $\displaystyle R_{\ell}(h_{t})$ $\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{h_{t}}(h_{t}-s)P^{\prime\prime}(\ell_{t}+s)\,\mathrm{d}s\geq 0,$ $\displaystyle R_{a}(j_{t})$ $\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{j_{t}}(j_{t}-s)P^{\prime\prime}(a_{t}-s)\,\mathrm{d}s\leq\frac{M_{t}}{2}j_{t}^{2},$

with $M_{t}(x)=\sup_{s\in[\ell_{t}(x),a_{t}(x)]}P^{\prime\prime}(s)$ . Imposing a trust region $0\leq j_{t}\leq\delta$ further gives $R_{a}(j_{t})\leq M_{t}\delta j_{t}/2$ . Therefore, the original nonlinear certification constraints are guaranteed by

(28) $\displaystyle F(\ell_{t})+[\mathcal{L}+\lambda(P^{\prime}(\ell_{t})-1)]h_{t}$ $\displaystyle\geq 0,$ $\displaystyle-F(a_{t})+[\mathcal{L}+\lambda(P^{\prime}(a_{t})-1-\tfrac{1}{2}M_{t}\delta)]j_{t}$ $\displaystyle\geq 0.$

Since $\ell_{t}$ , $a_{t}$ , and $M_{t}$ are fixed during each iteration, these conditions are affine in $h_{t}$ and $j_{t}$ . Together with the linear width-reduction objective and monotonicity constraints, they yield a linear program after finite-dimensional representation and continuous certification. Thus, the refinement extends to general offspring distributions while preserving the validity and nesting of the certified envelopes.

Finite-dimensional certified optimization.

We represent the envelopes using cubic B-splines,

$\ell(x)=\sum_{i}c_{i}^{\ell}\phi_{i}(x)$ and

$a(x)=\sum_{i}c_{i}^{a}\phi_{i}(x)$ , with their coefficients as optimization variables. Although Eq. () is affine in the corrections, it imposes infinitely many spatial constraints. The following theorem provides a finite-dimensional certification. On each spline cell, we express the affine residuals and ordering constraints in the Bernstein basis, enforcing nonnegativity of their coefficients; range and polynomial boundary constraints are handled analogously. These finitely many sufficient linear inequalities certify the PDE constraints throughout the domain while preserving monotone envelope refinement.

28

For nonrectangular domains, we may restrict these certificates to a decomposition of each cell intersected with $\Omega$ , using tensor-product or triangular Bernstein bases on the resulting pieces. This changes the sufficient finite constraints, while retaining the same globally $C^{2}$ spline representation and continuous PDE inequalities on $\Omega$ . Therefore, the resulting refinement is a linear program with continuous, rather than pointwise, certification. The Bernstein constraints yields a conservative feasible set. The envelopes are constructed once and reused across full-field evaluations, amortizing their preprocessing cost over all queries.

4.2.

Although the envelope transformation reduces branching complexity, sampling its spatially varying transition weights introduces additional overhead. We employ three complementary optimizations to reduce this cost while preserving the exact transition law.

Adaptive screening.

The screened-kernel representation allows an adjustable parameter $\mu\in[0,\lambda]$ . Using Eq. (), the interior weight $W_{\mu}=\lambda\omega_{I}-(\lambda-\mu)d$ , yielding

3

(29) $\displaystyle W_{\mu}=r_{\ell}+r_{a}+\lambda\sum_{j=2}^{K}C_{j}+[\mu-\lambda+\lambda P^{\prime}(\ell)]d.$

This decomposition shows that changing $\mu$ affects only the single-offspring continuation weight, leaving termination and genuine reproduction weights unchanged. Their nonnegativity is preserved by choosing $\mu_{B}=\lambda\max\{0,1-P^{\prime}(\underline{\ell}_{B})\}$ , where $\underline{\ell}_{B}$ is a certified lower bound over the sphere. A smaller $\mu_{B}$ increases the sphere-exit probability, potentially reducing expensive interior proposals without altering the represented solution.

Spatially adaptive majorants.

Instead of using global rejection bounds, we independently bound the exit and interior weights by $M_{E}\geq\sup_{\partial B}d$ and $M_{I}\geq\sup_{B}W_{\mu}$ . Their proposal masses are $q_{\mu}M_{E}$ and $m_{\mu}M_{I}$ , where $q_{\mu}=\int_{\partial B}H_{\mu}$ and $m_{\mu}=\int_{B}G_{\mu}$ . The corresponding acceptance probabilities are $d(y)/M_{E}$ and $W_{\mu}(y)/M_{I}$ . We obtain tight local bounds from the spline cells intersecting each sphere and accelerate their aggregation using range-minimum/maximum queries (RMQ), reducing rejection without changing the accepted distribution.

Lazy evaluation.

Even with tighter proposals, computing the exact envelope weights for every candidate is unnecessary. We first compare the rejection threshold against inexpensive local lower and upper bounds: candidates are accepted or rejected immediately when these bounds determine the outcome, and full spline evaluation is performed only otherwise. Green-kernel sampling is deferred until an interior proposal is selected, while reusable kernel quantities are cached. Thus, most inexpensive decisions avoid the cost of exact weight evaluation, and the savings accumulate across repeated transitions in the branching tree.

Spectral-workload fallback.

Envelope construction incurs a one-time cost that may outweigh its sampling benefits. Motivated by the near-critical BBM work scaling $(1-\rho)^{-1}$ , where $\rho=\lambda(P^{\prime}(1)-1)/\lambda_{1}<1$ , we define a spectral-workload indicator for $Q$ queries at target RMSE $\varepsilon$ :

(30) $\mathcal{W}=\frac{Q}{\varepsilon^{2}}\frac{\rho}{1-\rho}.$

We activate WiE only when $\rho\geq\rho_{0}$ and $\mathcal{W}\geq A$ , with $\rho_{0}=0.8$ and $A=10^{8}$ calibrated empirically across four scenes (Figure ). This pilot-free criterion avoids unnecessary preprocessing, while imperfect fallback decisions affect efficiency but not correctness.

Spline resolution.

Table (a) examines spatial resolution and geometric certification. The earlier implementation certifies the entire bounding square, including regions outside the PDE domain and inside holes. We instead clip certificate cells to the original polygon: intact or axis-aligned pieces use tensor-product Bernstein coefficients, and oblique pieces use triangular Bernstein coefficients. Both coefficient vectors are restricted to $[-2,2]$ to suppress large, weakly constrained exterior modes. Refinement iterations.

We allow up to 12 updates, retaining $d\geq 0.003$ and the upper-correction limit $0.075$ . We stop after two successive width reductions below $10^{-6}$ , or return the last valid pair when the LP budget or numerical checks fail; the actual accepted count is reported. If the full polynomial LP accepts no update, we retry from the same initialization using conservative cellwise scalar bounds on the residuals and $P^{\prime}$ ; both attempts are included in construction cost. Table (b) tests the returned pairs with fixed queries, sample count, seeds, and rejection-bound grid. At $k=24$ , the six non-square cases reduce mean width by 53–87% relative to the earlier coarse result. Relative to their common initialization, their sampling time–variance efficiency improves by $2.06$ – $23.13\times$ , while additional construction costs $298$ – $600$ CPU seconds. Thus finer envelopes improve sampling in these tests, but need sufficient reuse to offset preprocessing. The L-shaped case attains a smaller mean width at $k=12$ than at $k=24$ ; the latter uses the conservative fallback, and these finite-budget results do not imply monotonic improvement with resolution. These results diagnose envelope construction rather than changing the variable transformation underlying WiE. All cases use the general-PGF kernel; Figure  retains the earlier specialized binary implementation.

Sampling optimization ablation.

Figure  isolates Bernstein squeeze and RMQ using the same certified envelopes and random paths ( $\rho=0.98$ ). Squeeze reduces full spline evaluations from $14$ – $17$ to $2.5$ – $4.7$ per root sample; disabling it increases CPU time by $6.9$ – $15.6\%$ . Crucially, these optimizations leave the sampled estimator unchanged; the improvements arise from cheaper decisions rather than a different probability law.

Envelope quality and evaluation cost.

We further compare analytic affine envelopes with the final output of monotone B-spline construction on six meshes (Table ), using the same PDE, height-dependent boundary data, $\lambda=2.1\widehat{\lambda}_{1}$ , and boundary tolerance as above. The affine pair is $(\ell,a)=(0,h)$ . Cubic tensor-product splines use $9^{3}$ coefficients per envelope, start from $(0,0.9)$ , and allow up to eight refinement rounds, with a 60-second limit per LP. The 2,048 training points are independent of the 48 evaluation queries. Both representations use the same product estimator and exact termination after a zero factor.

6

At fixed $N=1{,}024$ , the five valid final spline configurations reduce the measured single-sample variance by $5.4$ – $21.0\%$ , but require $1.63$ – $4.05\times$ the sampling CPU time of the affine baseline, even before construction costs. Representing the identical affine envelopes as splines also increases sampling time by $1.17$ – $1.57\times$ , isolating representation and evaluation overhead. Fandisk and Spot accept no refinement and retain the initial envelope; the final Armadillo configuration requires event-probability repairs and is excluded from valid performance comparisons.

These results distinguish the variance bound from realized efficiency. The final spline envelopes have larger mean widths than the affine baseline; on Bunny, for example, the means are $0.582$ and $0.494$ , respectively, despite the lower measured spline variance. Equation () remains a valid worst-case bound, but when attainable envelopes remain broad, it can provide limited guidance for predicting actual variance or selecting the fastest representation. Lower measured variance alone is also insufficient: its benefit must offset the cost of sampling and envelope construction. For these tests, inexpensive analytic affine envelopes offer the better computational tradeoff while retaining WiE’s envelope transformation.

6.

WiE demonstrates that certified solution bounds can reshape branching dynamics rather than merely prune existing trees. While the transformation preserves unbiasedness, its efficiency depends on envelope quality and sampling acceptance rates. Constructing certified envelopes incurs preprocessing costs, making WiE less advantageous for low branching intensities or limited query workloads. Our spectral-workload fallback mitigates this overhead but relies on empirical calibration. Moreover, the near-critical complexity guarantee bounds expected reproduction events rather than total runtime. Extensions to manifold and parabolic PDEs demonstrate broader applicability, although projected walks inherit geometric approximation errors and space-time sampling introduces additional costs. Future work may include higher-dimensional certification and more efficient envelope optimization directly targeting computational work.

item.title: Stable Signer V3：用 4D 可变形基元泼溅做手语数字人 ｜ Stable Signer V3: 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting Is All You Need for Sign Language Production
item.description:
一句话：以 4D 可变形基元泼溅构建高分辨率手语虚拟人，补齐表情、身份形变与细节三个短板。

要点：

  • 共享面部基元泼溅，用可迁移的超二次曲面基元实现更丰富的表情控制
  • 测试时身体基元修正，解决身份相关的形变不准
  • 保留细粒度外观细节，支持交互式高分辨率渲染

为什么值得看：高保真角色与面部动画的一条可行路线：「共享基元 + 测试时个体化」，可迁移到虚拟角色与数字人系统。

中文摘要：Stable Signer V3 是一个基于 4D 可变形基元泼溅的交互式高分辨率手语虚拟人系统。它针对现有方案的三点不足：面部表情受限、身份相关的身体形变不准、细节丢失。作者引入共享面部基元泼溅，用可迁移的超二次曲面基元实现更丰富的表情控制；用测试时身体基元修正身份形变；同时保留细节。整体在实时性与保真度之间取得了新的平衡点。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

Stable Signer V3: 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting Is All You

Need for Sign Language Production

Sen Fang

Liwei Che

Dimitris N. Metaxas

Rutgers University

Affiliation: Affiliation:

https://signerx.github.io/Stable-Signer-V3

Abstract

We present , an interactive high-resolution sign language avatar system built on .

It addresses three limitations of existing avatars: restricted facial expression, inaccurate identity-specific body deformation, and loss of fine appearance details.

adds transferable superquadric primitives for richer expression control; learns an identity-specific virtual muscle layer for more faithful motion; and uses TunnelingNet to recover identity-specific high-resolution details.

Both test-time modules are optimized once per signer identity; inference then runs entirely from the stored identity parameters.

Together, they reduce facial geometry error by 71.4%, body-boundary error by 35.1% across ten identities, and high-resolution RGB reconstruction error by 24.2% on held-out evaluations, while retaining interactive streaming.Stable Signer V34D Deformable Primitive SplattingShared Face Primitive SplattingTest-Time Body Primitive SplattingTest-Time Tunneling Super-Resolution

1

Sign language production aims to translate text or lexical sequences into intelligible, natural, and expressive signing videos .

Sign language conveys information through coordinated manual gestures, facial expressions, head poses, and body movements .

A practical production system must therefore go beyond predicting skeletons or parametric poses: it must consistently express these motions through avatars with diverse identities and appearances, preserve subtle expressions and visual details, and meet the latency requirements of interactive applications .[, , ]

Existing approaches broadly follow two routes.

synthesizes signing videos from intermediate poses with pose-conditioned image or video generation models .

predicts language-conditioned 3D signing motion and uses it to animate explicit characters .

Pose-guided human-video models provide additional tools for this pipeline .

Dictionary-based production also exploits reusable signing segments and their transitions .

Pose generation models provide structured representations of signing motion .

Within these pipelines, 3D Gaussian splatting  enables efficient rendering, with recent extensions supporting signing avatars  and real-time upper-body animation .

Fine-grained signing remains a central rendering challenge even with accurate 3D pose prediction and fast rendering.

The resulting motion is jointly constrained by the local expressiveness of the parametric human model, the compatibility between template deformation and individual geometry, and the image decoder’s ability to reconstruct fine details.

We investigate how compact adaptation mechanisms can improve signing expression by building on existing motion and avatar priors.Text2Pose2Video[, , , , , , ]

Three challenges motivate this work.

First, the compact expression spaces of parametric face models such as FLAME  suppress subtle local motion and impose a geometric ceiling on facial detail.

Second, shared skinning and deformation rules cannot consistently accommodate identity-specific body shape and local surface motion . An avatar that appears plausible in its reference pose can therefore develop local shape errors as the pose changes.

Third, general-purpose decoders can discard identity-specific high-frequency details when reconstructing images from compact Gaussian features .

These challenges concern facial control, identity-specific body deformation, and high-resolution appearance, respectively.

Together, they limit the quality of existing sign language production systems.[]

30

[, , , ]

77

To address these challenges, we introduce , a sign language production system based on .

Our key idea is to introduce a learnable local deformation layer between the parametric human model and the avatar, separating shared facial motion capabilities from identity-specific body and appearance adaptation.

We instantiate the deformable primitives as superquadrics, allowing local residual deformations to vary with pose and expression while preserving the existing human control interface and avatar bindings.

Given text or gloss input, the system uses SignSparK  for motion completion and GUAVA  for avatar initialization and feature rendering.

A shared facial layer learns local residual deformations driven by FLAME expression, jaw, and eye controls and transfers them to the avatar through surface bindings.

For the body, a pose-conditioned virtual muscle layer is fitted to each identity from reference videos; it corrects geometry before skinning so that bound Gaussians follow the adjusted surface, with displacement and smoothness constraints discouraging implausible deformations.

For appearance, an independently normalized Softmax tunneling path uses terminal decoder semantics to learn identity-specific high-resolution detail while preserving the early Gaussian feature pathway.

Test-time adaptation forms a one-time per-identity character-preparation stage. The resulting body and detail parameters serve every subsequent sequence, cleanly separating identity adaptation from online generation.Stable Signer V34D Deformable Primitive Splatting[]

34

[]

77

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

•

A shared deformable primitive layer enables more complex and controllable facial expressions.Shared Face Primitive Splatting.

•

An identity-specific virtual muscle layer adapts body deformation from reference videos while keeping the avatar generation backbone frozen.Test-Time Body Primitive Splatting.

•

A late tunneling path learns identity-specific high-resolution detail from reference videos and stores it in the deployed decoder.Test-Time Tunneling Super-Resolution.

2

Resources such as WLASL , How2Sign , JWSign , and YouTube-SL-25  support research across lexical signs, continuous signing, and multiple languages.

Pose-conditioned video synthesis has been explored through Text2Sign , SignSynth , and Everybody Sign Now , with subsequent work on appearance control, large-scale co-articulation, and diffusion-based synthesis .

Broader human-video synthesis develops pose-guided generation through DreaMoving , Follow Your Pose , and MimicMotion , with ControlVideo  and Wan-Animate  further exploring controllable video generation and character animation.

The 3D route combines signing-motion generation  with controllable avatar rendering .

For motion generation, some methods retrieve and concatenate signing clips from existing dictionaries , while others learn to predict continuous motion from language inputs using progressive prediction or motion primitives .

Motion modeling has also explored adversarial training, skeletal graph structure, and non-autoregressive generation .

Related text-to-human-motion research studies diffusion-based synthesis and language-like motion modeling , providing a broader context for language-conditioned animation.

Recent motion generators explore discrete diffusion for gloss-to-pose synthesis , autoregressive motion tokens , and multilingual generation from text and prompts .

SignSparK  combines sparse keyframe control with conditional flow matching to generate dense 3D signing motion.

Appearance transfer in skeletal pose sequences further studies how signer-specific characteristics can be changed while retaining signing motion .

Together, these directions address motion accuracy, co-articulation, appearance control, and efficient generation .

We build on this motion completion capability and focus on facial, body, and appearance adaptation for personalized avatar rendering.Sign Language Production.[]

SMPL-X  provides joint body, hand, and facial controls for animatable humans, while FLAME  models facial shape, expression, and articulation.

These parametric representations support pose-driven signing avatars .

Whole-body reconstruction methods, including SMPLer-X and component-aware mesh recovery , and dedicated hand reconstruction  support detailed avatar controls; DWPose provides complementary whole-body keypoint estimates .

Complementary work improves 3D pose estimation for sign language  and resolves hand-to-hand intersections , supporting more reliable motion inputs.

Accurate facial and body motion is particularly relevant to signing, where non-manual cues contribute to meaning .

Building on 3D Gaussian splatting , SplattingAvatar  embeds Gaussians on a deformable mesh surface, while GART  learns forward skinning and latent bones to capture articulated and non-rigid motion.

Articulated Gaussian models further explore cage-based deformation in D3GA , monocular human reconstruction in GauHuman , and efficient human rendering in ASH and HiFi4G .

Related efforts address monocular Gaussian avatar reconstruction in GVA , image-based body estimation in GST , and generalizable sparse-view synthesis in GHG .

Expressive avatar reconstruction is also studied by X-Avatar  and EVA , with EVA learning Gaussian human avatars from monocular RGB video.

SignSplat  adapts Gaussian avatars to signing through sequence-level mesh fitting and Gaussian regularization, emphasizing accurate hands and facial expressions.

We retain structured human controls and surface bindings while adding a shared facial residual layer and identity-specific body deformation.3D Humans and Gaussian Avatars for Sign Language.[]

Video-based character reconstruction has developed through HumanNeRF  and NeuMan , with Vid2Avatar exploring self-supervised scene decomposition for videos in the wild .

Efficient character preparation is explored by InstantAvatar , which learns avatars from monocular video.

Subject-specific optimization can recover detailed avatar appearance: Gaussian Head Avatar  jointly learns neutral Gaussians and an expression-driven deformation field for high-fidelity 2K head rendering.

Reference-conditioned image and video synthesis transfers appearance from exemplar images .

High-resolution conditional synthesis and latent diffusion provide complementary image-generation frameworks , with ControlNet  and ControlNeXt  exploring additional conditioning for image and video generation.

For 3D avatars, GUAVA  predicts an animatable upper-body Gaussian avatar from a single image and refines rendered features with a neural decoder.

Lightweight adaptation offers a way to reuse pretrained representations: LoRA  learns low-rank weight updates, and LLaMA-Adapter  introduces new conditioning through zero-initialized attention.

Adapters also connect pretrained visual representations to dense prediction tasks .

These adaptation mechanisms motivate compact trainable paths around a frozen backbone.

We combine generalizable avatar initialization with identity-specific adaptation of body geometry and high-resolution appearance.

Character reference videos supervise a body deformation layer and a detail module at the decoder’s terminal stage, with the pretrained backbone held fixed.

Both modules are optimized once per signer, and online signing directly reuses the stored parameters.Personalized Avatars and Test-Time Training.[]

4

: Figure 2Overview of Stable Signer V3. Motion controls drive an avatar through deformable primitives. Gaussian feature splatting and a tunneling-enhanced decoder produce high-resolution signing videos.

3

3.1

Given text or gloss input, SignSparK  completes dictionary-retrieved sparse poses into body, hand, and facial controls $\{\mathbf{q}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ . GUAVA  initializes a surface-bound Gaussian avatar from a reference image. We augment this pipeline with shared facial deformation and identity-specific body and appearance adaptation.[]

34

[]

77

For signer $s$ , aligned reference images, controls, and cameras $\mathcal{V}_{s}=\{I_{t},\mathbf{q}_{t},\pi_{t}\}$ supervise image formation:

$\widehat{I}_{t}=\mathcal{D}_{\psi_{s}}\!\left(\mathcal{R}_{\pi_{t}}\!\left[\mathcal{G}_{s}(\mathbf{q}_{t};\phi,\theta_{s})\right]\right),$ (1)

where $\phi$ is the shared facial controller, $\theta_{s}$ is the body adaptation, and $\mathcal{G}_{s}$ transports Gaussians with the deformed surface. The rasterizer $\mathcal{R}$ projects Gaussian features, and $\mathcal{D}_{\psi_{s}}$ decodes them into high-resolution RGB. Adaptation occurs once per identity; inference runs from stored parameters.

3.2

Here denotes pose- and time-conditioned primitive transformations across motion sequences.

A sparse field blends control-dependent affine residuals over superquadric supports. Primitive $k$ has center $\mathbf{c}_{k}$ , orthonormal frame $\mathbf{R}_{k}$ , positive axis lengths $\mathbf{a}_{k}$ , and normalized distance4D

$d_{k}(\mathbf{x})=\left\|\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{a}_{k})^{-1}\mathbf{R}_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}_{k})\right\|_{4}.$ (2)

The level set $d_{k}(\mathbf{x})=1$ defines a superellipsoid with fixed shape exponents. Centers are initialized in bilateral pairs, and local surface covariance determines orientations and scales. The supports remain fixed during controller learning. Each surface sample receives a sparse neighborhood $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x})$ with weights

$w_{k}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\exp[-2d_{k}(\mathbf{x})^{2}]}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x})}\exp[-2d_{j}(\mathbf{x})^{2}]}.$ (3)

Fixed reference-surface bindings blend controller-predicted affine residuals $(\mathbf{A}_{k,t},\mathbf{b}_{k,t})$ :

$\Delta\mathbf{x}_{t}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x})}w_{k}(\mathbf{x})\left[\mathbf{A}_{k,t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{c}_{k})+\mathbf{b}_{k,t}\right],$ (4)

Here $\mathbf{x}_{t}$ uses local coordinates. Zero-initialized controller outputs preserve geometry. The field deforms the surface, while bound Gaussians supply appearance.

: Figure 3Deformation and detail adaptation. (a) Shared facial primitives learn geometric residuals with FLAME supervision. (b) Identity-specific body primitives adapt the avatar carrier. (c) A late Softmax tunneling pathway learns high-resolution appearance. Dashed arrows denote training supervision; solid arrows denote inference.

3.3

The shared facial field is conditioned on

$\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{face}}_{t}=[\mathbf{e}_{t},\mathbf{j}_{t},\mathbf{o}_{t},\boldsymbol{\ell}_{t}],$ (5)

comprising 50 expression coefficients, three jaw parameters, six eye-pose parameters, and two eyelid controls. Global head orientation is handled by the body rig. A multilayer perceptron maps normalized facial controls to the affine residuals in Eq. . Common facial surface correspondences provide the interface for transferring the shared controller across identities.

4

Paired geometry from a tracked FLAME sequence uses ten expression coefficients for the base and fifty for the target, with other controls identical. For corresponding surface samples $\mathbf{x}_{ti}$ and $\mathbf{y}_{ti}$ , we minimize

$\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{face}}={}&\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum_{(t,i)\in\Omega}\omega_{i}\rho(\mathbf{x}_{ti}+\Delta\mathbf{x}_{ti}-\mathbf{y}_{ti})\\

&+\lambda_{f}\mathbb{E}_{t}\|\mathbf{T}_{t}\|_{F}^{2},\end{split}$ (6)

where $\rho$ is a smooth $L_{1}$ penalty, $\Omega$ indexes training samples, and $\mathbf{T}_{t}$ collects affine coefficients. Weights $\omega_{i}$ emphasize lips and eyes. Appearance, opacity, and the decoder remain frozen; compatible facial bindings transfer the controller across identities.

3.4

An identity-specific virtual muscle layer covers the torso, shoulders, arms, and wrists. Static and pose-dependent affine corrections capture individual surface motion:

$\mathbf{T}_{s,t}=\tanh\!\left(\mathbf{T}^{\mathrm{static}}_{s}+f_{\theta_{s}}(\overline{\mathbf{p}}_{t})\right),$ (7)

where $\overline{\mathbf{p}}_{t}$ is the normalized 63-dimensional body pose. Static and dynamic components capture shape and articulation effects, with bounded coefficients limiting distortion.

The blended field modifies the canonical carrier before skinning:

$\widetilde{\mathbf{V}}_{s,t}=\operatorname{LBS}\!\left(\mathbf{V}^{\mathrm{can}}_{s}+\mathcal{S}(\Delta\mathbf{V}_{s,t}),\mathbf{q}_{t}\right).$ (8)

Here $\mathcal{S}$ smooths offsets along body mesh edges, preserving the head, hands, and motion controls. Template and UV Gaussians follow corrected vertices and parent triangles, respectively.

Differentiable rendering supervises a dilated visibility region of body-bound Gaussians. Raw and decoded RGB, gradients, SSIM , silhouette, and boundary losses enforce video alignment:[]

67

$\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{body}}={}&\lambda_{r}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{raw}}+\lambda_{c}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rgb}}+\lambda_{g}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{grad}}+\lambda_{s}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ssim}}\\

&+\lambda_{m}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mask}}+\lambda_{b}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{boundary}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}.\end{split}$ (9)

Regularization penalizes affine magnitude, neighboring translations, and mean vertex displacement. The avatar generator, appearance, and renderer remain frozen. Held-out reconstruction guides selection.

3.5

A late Softmax tunnel adapts terminal decoder features into identity-specific detail before RGB prediction.

Let $\mathbf{h}_{t}(\mathbf{p})$ be the terminal feature at location $\mathbf{p}$ . Learnable spatial keys and values $\{\mathbf{k}_{s,n},\mathbf{v}_{s,n}\}_{n=1}^{N}$ are initialized from reference frames and optimized by video reconstruction. Interpolation to the feature resolution gives

$\displaystyle\alpha_{t,n}(\mathbf{p})$ $\displaystyle=\frac{\exp[\mathbf{z}_{t}(\mathbf{p})^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{k}_{s,n}(\mathbf{p})/\sqrt{r}]}{\sum_{m=1}^{N}\exp[\mathbf{z}_{t}(\mathbf{p})^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{k}_{s,m}(\mathbf{p})/\sqrt{r}]},$ (10) $\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}(\mathbf{p})$ $\displaystyle=\mathbf{h}_{t}(\mathbf{p})+W_{o}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\alpha_{t,n}(\mathbf{p})\mathbf{v}_{s,n}(\mathbf{p}),$ (11)

Here $N$ is the number of memory slots, $\mathbf{z}_{t}(\mathbf{p})=W_{q}\mathbf{h}_{t}(\mathbf{p})$ , and $r$ is the query/key dimension. Projections $W_{q}$ and $W_{o}$ map into and out of the tunnel, while $\alpha_{t,n}$ weights slot $n$ . Softmax normalizes slots per location; zero-initialized $W_{o}$ preserves the original feature path.

Low-rank updates $\Delta W=BA$ , with trainable factors $A$ and $B$ , complement the tunnel with pretrained weights frozen. Training and inference use one StyleUNet  pass; stored identity memory supplies the deployed inference path.[]

66

High-resolution reconstruction.

Let $J_{t}$ be the decoded RGB image and $\mathcal{U}_{q}$ denote spatial upsampling by factor $q$ . The intermediate reconstruction is

$\widehat{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{mid}}=\mathcal{U}_{q}(J_{t})+\mathcal{H}_{s}(\widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t},J_{t}),$ (12)

where $\mathcal{H}_{s}$ is an identity-adapted PixelShuffle residual head. A shared fully convolutional head refines aligned native-resolution crops for 4K output. High-resolution target patches preserve supervision detail.

Appearance objective.

We learn appearance parameters from aligned video frames with fixed geometry and Gaussian features. Intermediate-resolution supervision combines RGB, image-gradient, multiscale high-pass, detail-band, local-contrast, perceptual, and low-frequency penalties. The native-resolution head receives RGB, gradient, high-pass, and local-detail supervision:

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{detail}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{mid}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mid}}+\mathbb{E}_{t,\mathcal{P}}\sum_{a}\lambda_{a}\mathcal{L}_{a}(\widehat{I}_{t}^{\mathcal{P}},I_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}),$ (13)

Here $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mid}}$ is the intermediate loss above; $\lambda_{\mathrm{mid}}$ and $\lambda_{a}$ are nonnegative weights. The crop $\mathcal{P}$ is shared by prediction and target, and $a$ indexes the native-resolution loss terms. Patch sampling preserves target-frequency information while bounding training memory. Body and detail adaptation are optimized with their respective frozen components, yielding a geometric controller and an appearance decoder for each identity. Online signing combines these modules with the shared facial field and newly generated motion.

: Figure 4Face primitive reconstruction on a held-out frame. Top: restricted FLAME. Bottom: SQ-corrected geometry, colored by primitive assignment. The second column amplifies surface deviations from the target by $5\times$ for visibility. The third column shows the full-expression target; the last shows unamplified geometric error on a shared scale (darker indicates larger error).

: Figure 5Test-time body adaptation. Frozen GUAVA (top) and identity-specific Body SQ (bottom). Columns show the rendered avatar, reference frame with adapted SQ patches overlaid at 60% opacity, geometric carrier, target, and RGB error on a shared scale. The top-row reference has no SQ overlay. We show the held-out moment with the largest body-region RGB error reduction in this clip.

4

4.1

The evaluation covers facial expression reconstruction, identity-specific body adaptation, and high-resolution detail recovery.

Controlled face and body studies use chronological 80%/20% training–evaluation splits and fixed optimization budgets; checkpoint selection uses the training segment exclusively. Detail adaptation is evaluated on held-out frames, and cross-method rendering uses identical poses, cameras, backgrounds, and target-defined crops for every method. Scores are first aggregated per identity and then macro-averaged.Data and protocol.

Facial geometry is measured by Euclidean point error in the native shared tracked coordinates. Body adaptation reports refined RGB L1, boundary L1, and SSIM . Rendering comparisons use foreground PSNR  together with SSIM and LPIPS  inside a shared ground-truth person crop. Runtime measurements distinguish independently warmed stage throughput from measured resident-pipeline wall time. Semantic preservation is evaluated through fixed back-translation using BLEU-4  and ROUGE-L F1  on poses re-extracted from the rendered RGB videos.Metrics.[]

67

[]

68

[]

82

[]

39

[]

31

4.2

We train the shared face layer on the tracked FLAME sequence provided with GUAVA , using a chronological 80%/20% training–evaluation split and a fixed optimization budget. The restricted FLAME carrier and the full-expression target share identical articulation, isolating the expression geometry that our layer must recover.[]

77

Table  reports Euclidean error over all retained head samples, including template- and UV-bound samples: mean head error falls from 1.267 to 0.362 mm (71.4%), and facial error falls from 1.492 to 0.518 mm. Figure  shows the held-out midpoint with a shared error scale and $5\times$ deviation magnification. The shared primitive controller reduces head error by 71.4% and recovers fine expression geometry across the face; region-wise results are provided in the supplement.

1

4

Average over the held-out 20% of the sequence. Head aggregates all retained samples; face and lip metrics use their semantic subsets. Held-out full-expression FLAME tracking provides the target geometry.Table 1: Face reconstruction error (mm, lower is better).

Baseline and Body SQ use the same chronological 80%/20% train–evaluation split for one identity. Both SQ variants share the adaptation budget and loss weights. Metrics are computed in the body region; RGB L1 uses refined renderings.Table 2: Body primitive count.

: Figure 6Detail adaptation. Frozen baseline, Adapter, and our tunneling decoder at the same timestamp. Circular insets magnify identical facial regions. The baseline is enlarged from 512 resolution; both adapted outputs are generated at 1024. Parentheses report mean held-out RGB L1 reductions relative to the frozen baseline.

4.3

Figure  compares frozen GUAVA, an Adapter, and our tunneling decoder through synchronized facial crops. The 512-resolution baseline is enlarged for display. Both adapted outputs are generated at 1024 resolution, and the visualization presents the combined effect of adaptation and native-resolution decoding. All trainable variants use the same frames, Gaussian features, targets, optimizer, and update budget. On held-out frames, Adapter reduces mean RGB L1 by 13.5%, while tunneling reduces it by 24.2% relative to the frozen baseline.

Table  reports warmed batch-one component throughput on a single Quadro RTX 8000. Motion synthesis and primitive deformation run at 198.7 and 320.9 FPS, while HD avatar rendering and 4K detail refinement reach 52.0 and 47.6 FPS. In the resident pipeline, stages overlap across streaming chunks. A warmed 784-frame, three-chunk text-to-HD-avatar run completes in 31.0 seconds wall time (25.3 generated FPS), including composition, motion synthesis, streamed rendering, encoding, and chunk concatenation. Body and detail adaptation are performed once for each new avatar and baked into the deployed model; subsequent sequences run directly from the baked parameters.Online efficiency.

3

Table  tests whether the proposed visual enhancement components alter the linguistic content of the output. Both configurations render the same motion sequence; the full configuration additionally activates shared face primitives, test-time body primitives, and detail tunneling. We re-extract signing poses from each rendered video and translate them with the same frozen back-translation model. Activating all three components raises BLEU-4 from 25.6450 to 26.8897 (4.9%) and ROUGE-L from 59.4771 to 61.7298 (3.8%). The complete enhancement stack therefore improves geometric and rendering fidelity while fully preserving the underlying signs.Back-translation evaluation.

Table  first compares our system with four reproducible open-source avatar methods at one shared held-out pose for each of four input reference videos. We compute PSNR inside the shared ground-truth foreground mask and SSIM/LPIPS within the same ground-truth person bounding box, then macro-average identities. The second block evaluates our identity-adapted renderer against frozen GUAVA using matched cached features and crops sampled directly from held-out 4K targets.Rendering fidelity.

5

The second block measures identity adaptation by comparing frozen GUAVA and our complete renderer on the same held-out subset from each of ten reference videos. Both methods receive identical cached Gaussian features, crop coordinates, and $768{\times}768$ crops sampled directly from the held-out 4K frames. Macro-averaged over identities, Stable Signer V3 raises PSNR from 19.418 to 21.790 dB and SSIM from 0.833 to 0.860, while reducing LPIPS from 0.245 to 0.226. This corresponds to a 2.372 dB PSNR gain and an 8.0% relative LPIPS reduction over the frozen renderer.

The shared framing makes facial detail, finger articulation, and garment boundaries directly comparable across columns. Across identities and poses, our method preserves facial character, articulated fingers, silhouettes, and garment boundaries more consistently than the reproduced baselines.

Macro-averaged results under two matched protocols: shared held-out poses for four identities (top) and crops sampled directly from held-out 4K targets for ten identities (bottom). PSNR uses GT foreground; SSIM and LPIPS use the shared GT person crop.Table 5: Rendering fidelity.

5

We presented Stable Signer V3, a sign language production framework combining shared facial primitives, test-time identity-specific body primitives, and a tunneling decoder for high-resolution appearance. Together, they unify expressive control and personalized rendering through a reusable deformable representation. Reference-video adaptation is performed once, after which the stored identity parameters drive subsequent signing sequences. On held-out evaluations, the three modules reduce head reconstruction error by 71.4%, body-boundary error by 35.1% across ten identities, and high-resolution RGB reconstruction error by 24.2%, while retaining interactive inference. Future work will broaden signer and motion coverage and include evaluation by proficient sign-language users.

We expand the evaluation protocols, component analyses, and deployment measurements presented in the main paper. Supervision and evaluation occupy temporally disjoint segments, and checkpoint selection uses the supervision segment exclusively. Paired methods share motion, camera, background, crop, and target data. The controlled face and body studies use fixed optimization budgets.

6.1

We evaluate facial deformation on the tracked FLAME sequence distributed with GUAVA . The first 80% trains the shared primitive controller, and the final 20% measures generalization to later motion. Restricted-FLAME and full-expression geometry share the tracked global pose, jaw, eye, and eyelid articulation, assigning their displacement directly to expression detail. We compute Euclidean error in the common tracked coordinates.[]

77

The controller contains $K{=}1{,}024$ local primitives, four-neighbor blending, and a compact residual MLP with 2.42M trainable parameters. We optimize it for 1,200 iterations using batch size 8 and a learning rate of $2\!\times\!10^{-3}$ . Table  resolves the aggregate head error into semantic regions. Face primitives reduce error across the lips, eyes, forehead, and nose, confirming that the improvement spans the expressive facial surface.

6

Mean Euclidean point error on the held-out 20% of the tracked sequence. Both methods use identical articulation and coordinates.Table 6: Region-wise face reconstruction error.

6.2

The body capacity study uses a chronological 80%/20% split of one identity-specific reference video. We uniformly sample a fixed evaluation subset and train the $K{=}512$ and $K{=}1{,}024$ models for the same 249-step budget. Both configurations share four-neighbor blending, optimizer, supervision, and loss weights. Their objective combines raw and refined RGB reconstruction, silhouette and boundary alignment, image gradients, SSIM, anchor regularization, and spatial smoothness.

Table  further evaluates the final $K{=}1{,}024$ checkpoint over the complete held-out segment. With the carrier and renderer fixed, continued adaptation improves appearance and boundary alignment. Its 1.25-cm mean displacement shows that compact local corrections are sufficient to capture identity-specific body geometry.

7

The first three rows reproduce the controlled capacity study; the final row reports the converged model on the complete held-out segment.Table 7: Body adaptation over the held-out segment.

We then fit the same $K{=}1{,}024$ configuration independently to ten characters. Table  reports macro-averages over their complete held-out segments. Body primitives improve refined RGB L1, boundary L1, and SSIM for every character, demonstrating consistent per-character adaptation across the full identity set.

8

Macro-average over temporally held-out segments. The same model configuration and evaluation code are used for all identities.Table 8: Ten-identity body adaptation.

7

Native-resolution reference video supervises the detail module with the Gaussian predictor and StyleUNet  backbone fixed. Character preparation bakes the learned identity parameters into the decoder, and online sequences run directly through this personalized model. The design concentrates reference evidence into a one-time adaptation stage and preserves a single-stream inference path.[]

66

Table  compares the trainable alternatives under a shared 900-step budget. LoRA and Adapter both improve the frozen decoder; the independent late Softmax pathway achieves the largest reconstruction gain. Increasing memory from 64 to 128 slots adds only 0.08 dB. We therefore adopt rank-8 tunneling with 64 slots as the default operating point.

9

Every trainable method is evaluated after 900 update steps on the same identity, held-out frames, Gaussian features, and native-resolution targets.Table 9: Equal-budget detail adaptation.

At convergence, the selected 64-slot model reaches 0.0181 RGB L1 and 24.43 dB PSNR; the 128-slot model reaches 0.0178 and 24.48 dB. This 0.05-dB gap shows that 64 slots capture nearly all of the detail gain, supporting the selected default.

8

Table  reports native-4K results for all ten identities. Each renderer receives identical Gaussian features and deterministic aligned $768{\times}768$ crops from held-out 4K targets. We compute each identity score first and then macro-average, giving every character equal weight.

10

: Table 10Per-identity native-4K rendering fidelity. The adapted renderer improves all three metrics for every evaluated identity. Identity labels are anonymized and fixed across columns.

9

Stage throughput and latency.

On one Quadro RTX 8000, warmed batch-one throughput reaches 198.7 FPS for motion synthesis, 320.9 FPS for primitive deformation, 52.0 FPS for avatar rendering, and 47.6 FPS for 4K detail refinement. The resident pipeline overlaps stages across chunks. A warmed 784-frame, three-chunk text-to-HD-avatar request completes in 31.0 seconds, yielding 25.3 FPS across composition, diffusion, streaming render, encoding, and concatenation. This wall-clock measurement captures the concurrency of the deployed pipeline.

One-time character preparation.

The shared face controller transfers directly across characters. Character preparation fits the body and detail modules once and stores them with the avatar. Each final $K{=}1{,}024$ body model contains 2.43M trainable parameters and occupies 9.6 MB. Across ten identities, body adaptation averages 40.2 minutes on one Quadro RTX 8000, with a 22.6–53.5 minute range driven mainly by clip length. Online inference loads the resulting character package directly.

Meaning of 4D deformable primitives.

In our formulation, indexes primitive transformations by pose and time throughout a motion sequence. The primitives supply local deformable support for the surface-bound Gaussian avatar, and Gaussian splatting rasterizes the resulting features. This factorization adds expressive local control to the pretrained parametric carrier while preserving its avatar representation and rendering path.4D

10

Figures  and  demonstrate the complete generation workflow in the Stable Signer V3 interface. A user can begin with English text, an instruction-conditioned prompt, or an editable gloss sequence, then select an avatar identity from its reference thumbnail. After a single prewarm operation, executes gloss composition, body, hand, and face motion synthesis, followed by Gaussian-avatar rendering. The interface streams intermediate results and exposes the generated SMPL-X motion for direct inspection. The same job can then be viewed as the Gaussian avatar on black or white backgrounds, while completed requests remain available under . This interface turns the full text-to-4K-avatar system into a short, inspectable workflow and requires no manual exchange of intermediate files.

一句话：以 4D 可变形基元泼溅构建高分辨率手语虚拟人，补齐表情、身份形变与细节三个短板。

要点：

  • 共享面部基元泼溅，用可迁移的超二次曲面基元实现更丰富的表情控制
  • 测试时身体基元修正，解决身份相关的形变不准
  • 保留细粒度外观细节，支持交互式高分辨率渲染

为什么值得看：高保真角色与面部动画的一条可行路线：「共享基元 + 测试时个体化」，可迁移到虚拟角色与数字人系统。

中文摘要：Stable Signer V3 是一个基于 4D 可变形基元泼溅的交互式高分辨率手语虚拟人系统。它针对现有方案的三点不足：面部表情受限、身份相关的身体形变不准、细节丢失。作者引入共享面部基元泼溅，用可迁移的超二次曲面基元实现更丰富的表情控制；用测试时身体基元修正身份形变；同时保留细节。整体在实时性与保真度之间取得了新的平衡点。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

Stable Signer V3: 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting Is All You

Need for Sign Language Production

Sen Fang

Liwei Che

Dimitris N. Metaxas

Rutgers University

Affiliation: Affiliation:

https://signerx.github.io/Stable-Signer-V3

Abstract

We present , an interactive high-resolution sign language avatar system built on .

It addresses three limitations of existing avatars: restricted facial expression, inaccurate identity-specific body deformation, and loss of fine appearance details.

adds transferable superquadric primitives for richer expression control; learns an identity-specific virtual muscle layer for more faithful motion; and uses TunnelingNet to recover identity-specific high-resolution details.

Both test-time modules are optimized once per signer identity; inference then runs entirely from the stored identity parameters.

Together, they reduce facial geometry error by 71.4%, body-boundary error by 35.1% across ten identities, and high-resolution RGB reconstruction error by 24.2% on held-out evaluations, while retaining interactive streaming.Stable Signer V34D Deformable Primitive SplattingShared Face Primitive SplattingTest-Time Body Primitive SplattingTest-Time Tunneling Super-Resolution

1

Sign language production aims to translate text or lexical sequences into intelligible, natural, and expressive signing videos .

Sign language conveys information through coordinated manual gestures, facial expressions, head poses, and body movements .

A practical production system must therefore go beyond predicting skeletons or parametric poses: it must consistently express these motions through avatars with diverse identities and appearances, preserve subtle expressions and visual details, and meet the latency requirements of interactive applications .[, , ]

Existing approaches broadly follow two routes.

synthesizes signing videos from intermediate poses with pose-conditioned image or video generation models .

predicts language-conditioned 3D signing motion and uses it to animate explicit characters .

Pose-guided human-video models provide additional tools for this pipeline .

Dictionary-based production also exploits reusable signing segments and their transitions .

Pose generation models provide structured representations of signing motion .

Within these pipelines, 3D Gaussian splatting  enables efficient rendering, with recent extensions supporting signing avatars  and real-time upper-body animation .

Fine-grained signing remains a central rendering challenge even with accurate 3D pose prediction and fast rendering.

The resulting motion is jointly constrained by the local expressiveness of the parametric human model, the compatibility between template deformation and individual geometry, and the image decoder’s ability to reconstruct fine details.

We investigate how compact adaptation mechanisms can improve signing expression by building on existing motion and avatar priors.Text2Pose2Video[, , , , , , ]

Three challenges motivate this work.

First, the compact expression spaces of parametric face models such as FLAME  suppress subtle local motion and impose a geometric ceiling on facial detail.

Second, shared skinning and deformation rules cannot consistently accommodate identity-specific body shape and local surface motion . An avatar that appears plausible in its reference pose can therefore develop local shape errors as the pose changes.

Third, general-purpose decoders can discard identity-specific high-frequency details when reconstructing images from compact Gaussian features .

These challenges concern facial control, identity-specific body deformation, and high-resolution appearance, respectively.

Together, they limit the quality of existing sign language production systems.[]

To address these challenges, we introduce , a sign language production system based on .

Our key idea is to introduce a learnable local deformation layer between the parametric human model and the avatar, separating shared facial motion capabilities from identity-specific body and appearance adaptation.

We instantiate the deformable primitives as superquadrics, allowing local residual deformations to vary with pose and expression while preserving the existing human control interface and avatar bindings.

Given text or gloss input, the system uses SignSparK  for motion completion and GUAVA  for avatar initialization and feature rendering.

A shared facial layer learns local residual deformations driven by FLAME expression, jaw, and eye controls and transfers them to the avatar through surface bindings.

For the body, a pose-conditioned virtual muscle layer is fitted to each identity from reference videos; it corrects geometry before skinning so that bound Gaussians follow the adjusted surface, with displacement and smoothness constraints discouraging implausible deformations.

For appearance, an independently normalized Softmax tunneling path uses terminal decoder semantics to learn identity-specific high-resolution detail while preserving the early Gaussian feature pathway.

Test-time adaptation forms a one-time per-identity character-preparation stage. The resulting body and detail parameters serve every subsequent sequence, cleanly separating identity adaptation from online generation.Stable Signer V34D Deformable Primitive Splatting[]

34

[]

77

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

•

A shared deformable primitive layer enables more complex and controllable facial expressions.Shared Face Primitive Splatting.

•

An identity-specific virtual muscle layer adapts body deformation from reference videos while keeping the avatar generation backbone frozen.Test-Time Body Primitive Splatting.

•

A late tunneling path learns identity-specific high-resolution detail from reference videos and stores it in the deployed decoder.Test-Time Tunneling Super-Resolution.

2

Resources such as WLASL , How2Sign , JWSign , and YouTube-SL-25  support research across lexical signs, continuous signing, and multiple languages.

Pose-conditioned video synthesis has been explored through Text2Sign , SignSynth , and Everybody Sign Now , with subsequent work on appearance control, large-scale co-articulation, and diffusion-based synthesis .

Broader human-video synthesis develops pose-guided generation through DreaMoving , Follow Your Pose , and MimicMotion , with ControlVideo  and Wan-Animate  further exploring controllable video generation and character animation.

The 3D route combines signing-motion generation  with controllable avatar rendering .

For motion generation, some methods retrieve and concatenate signing clips from existing dictionaries , while others learn to predict continuous motion from language inputs using progressive prediction or motion primitives .

Motion modeling has also explored adversarial training, skeletal graph structure, and non-autoregressive generation .

Related text-to-human-motion research studies diffusion-based synthesis and language-like motion modeling , providing a broader context for language-conditioned animation.

Recent motion generators explore discrete diffusion for gloss-to-pose synthesis , autoregressive motion tokens , and multilingual generation from text and prompts .

SignSparK  combines sparse keyframe control with conditional flow matching to generate dense 3D signing motion.

Appearance transfer in skeletal pose sequences further studies how signer-specific characteristics can be changed while retaining signing motion .

Together, these directions address motion accuracy, co-articulation, appearance control, and efficient generation .

We build on this motion completion capability and focus on facial, body, and appearance adaptation for personalized avatar rendering.Sign Language Production.[]

SMPL-X  provides joint body, hand, and facial controls for animatable humans, while FLAME  models facial shape, expression, and articulation.

These parametric representations support pose-driven signing avatars .

Whole-body reconstruction methods, including SMPLer-X and component-aware mesh recovery , and dedicated hand reconstruction  support detailed avatar controls; DWPose provides complementary whole-body keypoint estimates .

Complementary work improves 3D pose estimation for sign language  and resolves hand-to-hand intersections , supporting more reliable motion inputs.

Accurate facial and body motion is particularly relevant to signing, where non-manual cues contribute to meaning .

Building on 3D Gaussian splatting , SplattingAvatar  embeds Gaussians on a deformable mesh surface, while GART  learns forward skinning and latent bones to capture articulated and non-rigid motion.

Articulated Gaussian models further explore cage-based deformation in D3GA , monocular human reconstruction in GauHuman , and efficient human rendering in ASH and HiFi4G .

Related efforts address monocular Gaussian avatar reconstruction in GVA , image-based body estimation in GST , and generalizable sparse-view synthesis in GHG .

Expressive avatar reconstruction is also studied by X-Avatar  and EVA , with EVA learning Gaussian human avatars from monocular RGB video.

SignSplat  adapts Gaussian avatars to signing through sequence-level mesh fitting and Gaussian regularization, emphasizing accurate hands and facial expressions.

We retain structured human controls and surface bindings while adding a shared facial residual layer and identity-specific body deformation.3D Humans and Gaussian Avatars for Sign Language.[]

Video-based character reconstruction has developed through HumanNeRF  and NeuMan , with Vid2Avatar exploring self-supervised scene decomposition for videos in the wild .

Efficient character preparation is explored by InstantAvatar , which learns avatars from monocular video.

Subject-specific optimization can recover detailed avatar appearance: Gaussian Head Avatar  jointly learns neutral Gaussians and an expression-driven deformation field for high-fidelity 2K head rendering.

Reference-conditioned image and video synthesis transfers appearance from exemplar images .

High-resolution conditional synthesis and latent diffusion provide complementary image-generation frameworks , with ControlNet  and ControlNeXt  exploring additional conditioning for image and video generation.

For 3D avatars, GUAVA  predicts an animatable upper-body Gaussian avatar from a single image and refines rendered features with a neural decoder.

Lightweight adaptation offers a way to reuse pretrained representations: LoRA  learns low-rank weight updates, and LLaMA-Adapter  introduces new conditioning through zero-initialized attention.

Adapters also connect pretrained visual representations to dense prediction tasks .

These adaptation mechanisms motivate compact trainable paths around a frozen backbone.

We combine generalizable avatar initialization with identity-specific adaptation of body geometry and high-resolution appearance.

Character reference videos supervise a body deformation layer and a detail module at the decoder’s terminal stage, with the pretrained backbone held fixed.

Both modules are optimized once per signer, and online signing directly reuses the stored parameters.Personalized Avatars and Test-Time Training.[]

: Figure 2Overview of Stable Signer V3. Motion controls drive an avatar through deformable primitives. Gaussian feature splatting and a tunneling-enhanced decoder produce high-resolution signing videos.

3

3.1

Given text or gloss input, SignSparK  completes dictionary-retrieved sparse poses into body, hand, and facial controls $\{\mathbf{q}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}$ . GUAVA  initializes a surface-bound Gaussian avatar from a reference image. We augment this pipeline with shared facial deformation and identity-specific body and appearance adaptation.[]

34

[]

77

For signer $s$ , aligned reference images, controls, and cameras $\mathcal{V}_{s}=\{I_{t},\mathbf{q}_{t},\pi_{t}\}$ supervise image formation:

$\widehat{I}_{t}=\mathcal{D}_{\psi_{s}}\!\left(\mathcal{R}_{\pi_{t}}\!\left[\mathcal{G}_{s}(\mathbf{q}_{t};\phi,\theta_{s})\right]\right),$ (1)

where $\phi$ is the shared facial controller, $\theta_{s}$ is the body adaptation, and $\mathcal{G}_{s}$ transports Gaussians with the deformed surface. The rasterizer $\mathcal{R}$ projects Gaussian features, and $\mathcal{D}_{\psi_{s}}$ decodes them into high-resolution RGB. Adaptation occurs once per identity; inference runs from stored parameters.

3.2

Here denotes pose- and time-conditioned primitive transformations across motion sequences.

A sparse field blends control-dependent affine residuals over superquadric supports. Primitive $k$ has center $\mathbf{c}_{k}$ , orthonormal frame $\mathbf{R}_{k}$ , positive axis lengths $\mathbf{a}_{k}$ , and normalized distance4D

$d_{k}(\mathbf{x})=\left\|\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{a}_{k})^{-1}\mathbf{R}_{k}^{\mathsf{T}}(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{c}_{k})\right\|_{4}.$ (2)

The level set $d_{k}(\mathbf{x})=1$ defines a superellipsoid with fixed shape exponents. Centers are initialized in bilateral pairs, and local surface covariance determines orientations and scales. The supports remain fixed during controller learning. Each surface sample receives a sparse neighborhood $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x})$ with weights

$w_{k}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{\exp[-2d_{k}(\mathbf{x})^{2}]}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x})}\exp[-2d_{j}(\mathbf{x})^{2}]}.$ (3)

Fixed reference-surface bindings blend controller-predicted affine residuals $(\mathbf{A}_{k,t},\mathbf{b}_{k,t})$ :

$\Delta\mathbf{x}_{t}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x})}w_{k}(\mathbf{x})\left[\mathbf{A}_{k,t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\mathbf{c}_{k})+\mathbf{b}_{k,t}\right],$ (4)

Here $\mathbf{x}_{t}$ uses local coordinates. Zero-initialized controller outputs preserve geometry. The field deforms the surface, while bound Gaussians supply appearance.

: Figure 3Deformation and detail adaptation. (a) Shared facial primitives learn geometric residuals with FLAME supervision. (b) Identity-specific body primitives adapt the avatar carrier. (c) A late Softmax tunneling pathway learns high-resolution appearance. Dashed arrows denote training supervision; solid arrows denote inference.

3.3

The shared facial field is conditioned on

$\mathbf{u}^{\mathrm{face}}_{t}=[\mathbf{e}_{t},\mathbf{j}_{t},\mathbf{o}_{t},\boldsymbol{\ell}_{t}],$ (5)

comprising 50 expression coefficients, three jaw parameters, six eye-pose parameters, and two eyelid controls. Global head orientation is handled by the body rig. A multilayer perceptron maps normalized facial controls to the affine residuals in Eq. . Common facial surface correspondences provide the interface for transferring the shared controller across identities.

4

Paired geometry from a tracked FLAME sequence uses ten expression coefficients for the base and fifty for the target, with other controls identical. For corresponding surface samples $\mathbf{x}_{ti}$ and $\mathbf{y}_{ti}$ , we minimize

$\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{face}}={}&\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum_{(t,i)\in\Omega}\omega_{i}\rho(\mathbf{x}_{ti}+\Delta\mathbf{x}_{ti}-\mathbf{y}_{ti})\\

&+\lambda_{f}\mathbb{E}_{t}\|\mathbf{T}_{t}\|_{F}^{2},\end{split}$ (6)

where $\rho$ is a smooth $L_{1}$ penalty, $\Omega$ indexes training samples, and $\mathbf{T}_{t}$ collects affine coefficients. Weights $\omega_{i}$ emphasize lips and eyes. Appearance, opacity, and the decoder remain frozen; compatible facial bindings transfer the controller across identities.

3.4

An identity-specific virtual muscle layer covers the torso, shoulders, arms, and wrists. Static and pose-dependent affine corrections capture individual surface motion:

$\mathbf{T}_{s,t}=\tanh\!\left(\mathbf{T}^{\mathrm{static}}_{s}+f_{\theta_{s}}(\overline{\mathbf{p}}_{t})\right),$ (7)

where $\overline{\mathbf{p}}_{t}$ is the normalized 63-dimensional body pose. Static and dynamic components capture shape and articulation effects, with bounded coefficients limiting distortion.

The blended field modifies the canonical carrier before skinning:

$\widetilde{\mathbf{V}}_{s,t}=\operatorname{LBS}\!\left(\mathbf{V}^{\mathrm{can}}_{s}+\mathcal{S}(\Delta\mathbf{V}_{s,t}),\mathbf{q}_{t}\right).$ (8)

Here $\mathcal{S}$ smooths offsets along body mesh edges, preserving the head, hands, and motion controls. Template and UV Gaussians follow corrected vertices and parent triangles, respectively.

Differentiable rendering supervises a dilated visibility region of body-bound Gaussians. Raw and decoded RGB, gradients, SSIM , silhouette, and boundary losses enforce video alignment:[]

67

$\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{body}}={}&\lambda_{r}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{raw}}+\lambda_{c}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rgb}}+\lambda_{g}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{grad}}+\lambda_{s}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ssim}}\\

&+\lambda_{m}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mask}}+\lambda_{b}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{boundary}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}.\end{split}$ (9)

Regularization penalizes affine magnitude, neighboring translations, and mean vertex displacement. The avatar generator, appearance, and renderer remain frozen. Held-out reconstruction guides selection.

3.5

A late Softmax tunnel adapts terminal decoder features into identity-specific detail before RGB prediction.

Let $\mathbf{h}_{t}(\mathbf{p})$ be the terminal feature at location $\mathbf{p}$ . Learnable spatial keys and values $\{\mathbf{k}_{s,n},\mathbf{v}_{s,n}\}_{n=1}^{N}$ are initialized from reference frames and optimized by video reconstruction. Interpolation to the feature resolution gives

$\displaystyle\alpha_{t,n}(\mathbf{p})$ $\displaystyle=\frac{\exp[\mathbf{z}_{t}(\mathbf{p})^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{k}_{s,n}(\mathbf{p})/\sqrt{r}]}{\sum_{m=1}^{N}\exp[\mathbf{z}_{t}(\mathbf{p})^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{k}_{s,m}(\mathbf{p})/\sqrt{r}]},$ (10) $\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t}(\mathbf{p})$ $\displaystyle=\mathbf{h}_{t}(\mathbf{p})+W_{o}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\alpha_{t,n}(\mathbf{p})\mathbf{v}_{s,n}(\mathbf{p}),$ (11)

Here $N$ is the number of memory slots, $\mathbf{z}_{t}(\mathbf{p})=W_{q}\mathbf{h}_{t}(\mathbf{p})$ , and $r$ is the query/key dimension. Projections $W_{q}$ and $W_{o}$ map into and out of the tunnel, while $\alpha_{t,n}$ weights slot $n$ . Softmax normalizes slots per location; zero-initialized $W_{o}$ preserves the original feature path.

Low-rank updates $\Delta W=BA$ , with trainable factors $A$ and $B$ , complement the tunnel with pretrained weights frozen. Training and inference use one StyleUNet  pass; stored identity memory supplies the deployed inference path.[]

66

High-resolution reconstruction.

Let $J_{t}$ be the decoded RGB image and $\mathcal{U}_{q}$ denote spatial upsampling by factor $q$ . The intermediate reconstruction is

$\widehat{I}_{t}^{\mathrm{mid}}=\mathcal{U}_{q}(J_{t})+\mathcal{H}_{s}(\widetilde{\mathbf{h}}_{t},J_{t}),$ (12)

where $\mathcal{H}_{s}$ is an identity-adapted PixelShuffle residual head. A shared fully convolutional head refines aligned native-resolution crops for 4K output. High-resolution target patches preserve supervision detail.

Appearance objective.

We learn appearance parameters from aligned video frames with fixed geometry and Gaussian features. Intermediate-resolution supervision combines RGB, image-gradient, multiscale high-pass, detail-band, local-contrast, perceptual, and low-frequency penalties. The native-resolution head receives RGB, gradient, high-pass, and local-detail supervision:

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{detail}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{mid}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mid}}+\mathbb{E}_{t,\mathcal{P}}\sum_{a}\lambda_{a}\mathcal{L}_{a}(\widehat{I}_{t}^{\mathcal{P}},I_{t}^{\mathcal{P}}),$ (13)

Here $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{mid}}$ is the intermediate loss above; $\lambda_{\mathrm{mid}}$ and $\lambda_{a}$ are nonnegative weights. The crop $\mathcal{P}$ is shared by prediction and target, and $a$ indexes the native-resolution loss terms. Patch sampling preserves target-frequency information while bounding training memory. Body and detail adaptation are optimized with their respective frozen components, yielding a geometric controller and an appearance decoder for each identity. Online signing combines these modules with the shared facial field and newly generated motion.

5

We presented Stable Signer V3, a sign language production framework combining shared facial primitives, test-time identity-specific body primitives, and a tunneling decoder for high-resolution appearance. Together, they unify expressive control and personalized rendering through a reusable deformable representation. Reference-video adaptation is performed once, after which the stored identity parameters drive subsequent signing sequences. On held-out evaluations, the three modules reduce head reconstruction error by 71.4%, body-boundary error by 35.1% across ten identities, and high-resolution RGB reconstruction error by 24.2%, while retaining interactive inference. Future work will broaden signer and motion coverage and include evaluation by proficient sign-language users.

We expand the evaluation protocols, component analyses, and deployment measurements presented in the main paper. Supervision and evaluation occupy temporally disjoint segments, and checkpoint selection uses the supervision segment exclusively. Paired methods share motion, camera, background, crop, and target data. The controlled face and body studies use fixed optimization budgets.

6.1

We evaluate facial deformation on the tracked FLAME sequence distributed with GUAVA . The first 80% trains the shared primitive controller, and the final 20% measures generalization to later motion. Restricted-FLAME and full-expression geometry share the tracked global pose, jaw, eye, and eyelid articulation, assigning their displacement directly to expression detail. We compute Euclidean error in the common tracked coordinates.[]

77

The controller contains $K{=}1{,}024$ local primitives, four-neighbor blending, and a compact residual MLP with 2.42M trainable parameters. We optimize it for 1,200 iterations using batch size 8 and a learning rate of $2\!\times\!10^{-3}$ . Table  resolves the aggregate head error into semantic regions. Face primitives reduce error across the lips, eyes, forehead, and nose, confirming that the improvement spans the expressive facial surface.

The body capacity study uses a chronological 80%/20% split of one identity-specific reference video. We uniformly sample a fixed evaluation subset and train the $K{=}512$ and $K{=}1{,}024$ models for the same 249-step budget. Both configurations share four-neighbor blending, optimizer, supervision, and loss weights. Their objective combines raw and refined RGB reconstruction, silhouette and boundary alignment, image gradients, SSIM, anchor regularization, and spatial smoothness.

Table  further evaluates the final $K{=}1{,}024$ checkpoint over the complete held-out segment. With the carrier and renderer fixed, continued adaptation improves appearance and boundary alignment. Its 1.25-cm mean displacement shows that compact local corrections are sufficient to capture identity-specific body geometry.

The first three rows reproduce the controlled capacity study; the final row reports the converged model on the complete held-out segment.Table 7: Body adaptation over the held-out segment.

We then fit the same $K{=}1{,}024$ configuration independently to ten characters. Table  reports macro-averages over their complete held-out segments. Body primitives improve refined RGB L1, boundary L1, and SSIM for every character, demonstrating consistent per-character adaptation across the full identity set.

The design concentrates reference evidence into a one-time adaptation stage and preserves a single-stream inference path.[]
