III-BNeural Skinning Fields Autoencoder

We train a neural skinning fields autoencoder to predict spatially continuous skinning weights across diverse 3D shapes and discretizations. The resulting mesh-free representation supports the skinning-based real-time animation described in Sec. . Unlike existing neural subspace methods  that train a separate neural network for each object, our single feed-forward network generalizes across diverse objects, improving scalability and practicality.

III-D

[, ]

44

10

We use the transformer-based point cloud encoder Michelangelo  to extract a highly compressed latent set $\mathbf{F}_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d}$ for a given 3D shape via a cross-attention block and several self-attention blocks:Neural 3D Shape Encoding.[]

67

$\mathbf{F}_{s}=\mathrm{SelfAttn}^{(1:L)}(\mathrm{CrossAttn}(\mathbf{Q}_{s},\gamma(\mathbf{P}))),$ (2)

where $\mathbf{Q}_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d}$ is a set of learnable shape latent tokens, $\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 6}$ is the sampled surface point cloud with $N$ points, each point consisting of 3D coordinates and normals, $\gamma(\cdot)$ is point-wise positional encoding, $\mathrm{SelfAttn}^{(1:L)}(\cdot)$ indicates a stack of $L$ self-attention layers that iteratively improve the shape latent representation, $M$ is the number of latents, and $d$ is the dimension of each latent.

In practice, the shape encoder is pretrained on the ShapeNet dataset  via a signed distance field (SDF) reconstruction task  to learn generalizable geometric priors. We then freeze the encoder parameters during training to enhance efficiency.[]

7

[]

47

To obtain spatially continuous skinning fields, we decode the shape latent set $\mathbf{F}_{s}$ obtained from Eq. () into spatially varying skinning weights.

We first assign $m$ learnable skinning handle tokens $\mathbf{Q}_{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ , and then use a cross-attention block to extract a skinning handle latent set $\mathbf{F}_{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}$ from the shape latent set $\mathbf{F}_{s}$ :Neural Skinning Fields Decoding.

2

$\mathbf{F}_{h}=\mathrm{CrossAttn}(\mathbf{Q}_{h},\mathrm{SelfAttn}(\mathbf{F}_{s})).\vskip 3.00003pt$ (3)

Next, for any spatial query point $\mathbf{X}$ , we use another cross-attention block to extract a point-wise skinning feature $\mathbf{F}_{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ from the skinning handle latent set $\mathbf{F}_{h}$ :

$\mathbf{F}_{p}=\mathrm{CrossAttn}(\gamma(\mathbf{X}),\mathbf{F}_{h}).\vskip 3.00003pt$ (4)

Finally, we concatenate the point-wise skinning feature $\mathbf{F}_{p}$ with the positional encoding of the query point, and use a ResNet-style MLP to compute the skinning fields:

$\bm{W}(\mathbf{X})=\mathrm{MLP}(\mathbf{F}_{p}\oplus\gamma(\mathbf{X})),\vskip 1.99997pt$ (5)

where $\bm{W}(\mathbf{X})\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the skinning weight vector at point $\mathbf{X}$ , and $\oplus$ denotes the concatenation operator. To promote orthogonality among different skinning modes, we apply an Orthogonalization by Newton’s Iteration (ONI) module  at the final layer of the MLP, and we adopt ELU as the activation function in the MLP, which allows learning flexible and expressive skinning-based deformation subspaces without enforcing non-negativity on the learned skinning modes. We denote the full autoencoder by $\Phi_{\theta}$ and its skinning weight output at $\mathbf{X}$ by $\Phi_{\theta}(\mathbf{X})$ . The continuous fields can be queried throughout the object, while cubature points specify locations for physics-informed training and numerical integration.[]

26

In the classical Finite Element Method (FEM) , the object’s volume is typically discretized into a tetrahedral mesh  to facilitate numerical solutions of physical equations. Unlike triangle surface meshes commonly used for rendering, which only contain surface points, tetrahedral meshes include interior volumetric elements that better capture the object’s spatial structure. To train the neural skinning fields autoencoder, we sample cubature points both on the object’s surface and inside its volume, with each cubature point serving as a spatial query point $\mathbf{X}$ for computing the potential energy $E_{\textrm{pot}}$ during subspace learning and skinning-based real-time animation. This sampling captures volumetric deformation behavior that surface-only sampling cannot, in contrast to popular 3D Shape VAEs  that only sample surface points. To sample interior cubature points, we first convert the object’s surface mesh into a watertight mesh , then uniformly sample points in the voxelized spatial grid using ray tracing , and classify points as being outside the object if the ray intersects the surface mesh and the dot product with the normal is negative. For surface cubature points, we employ Sharp Edge Sampling (SES)  to better capture geometric details.Cubature Points Sampling.[]

III-CPhysics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning

To learn a deformation subspace mapping directly from static geometry without annotated skinning data or precomputed simulation trajectories, we train the neural skinning fields autoencoder with a Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning (PISSL) strategy. The learned skinning fields should be spatially smooth and mutually independent, while inducing low-energy deformations. We therefore formulate a self-supervised objective consisting of potential-energy, smoothness, and orthogonality terms:

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{subspace}}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\text{smooth}}(\theta)+\lambda_{\text{pot}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{pot}}(\theta)+\lambda_{\text{orth}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{orth}}(\theta),$ (6)

where $\lambda_{\text{pot}}$ and $\lambda_{\text{orth}}$ weight the potential-energy and orthogonality losses, respectively. The additional objective for rig-complementary learning is introduced in Sec. .

III-E

Evolution of neural skinning fields during optimization. Starting from disordered initial representations, our physics-informed self-supervised learning progressively organizes them into physically consistent, approximately orthogonal, and spatially smooth skinning results. For visualization, each skinning weight function $\bm{W}_{i}$ is divided by $\max|\bm{W}_{i}|$ to fall within $[-1,1]$ .Fig. 3:

To encourage physically plausible deformations, we construct a low-energy subspace  by minimizing the expected potential energy of deformations induced by randomly sampled subspace coordinates $\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{12m}$ :Physical Constraints.[]

49

$\mathcal{L}_{\text{pot}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}}[E_{\textrm{pot}}^{\theta}(\phi(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{z}))],\vskip 3.99994pt$ (7)

where $\mathbf{z}$ is defined in Sec. , and $\mathcal{N}=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mu^{2}\mathbf{I}_{12m})$ denotes a Gaussian distribution over $\mathbb{R}^{12m}$ with $\mu=0.2$ . The expectation is estimated by averaging the potential energy over sampled subspace coordinates within a training batch. Here, $E_{\textrm{pot}}^{\theta}(\phi(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{z}))$ denotes the object’s potential energy evaluated using the deformation map induced by $\mathbf{z}$ under the current network parameters $\theta$ , with spatial integration approximated using cubature points. During training, we linearly interpolate the potential energy computation from the linear elasticity  model to the Neo-Hookean  model to enhance training stability . Besides the low-energy constraint imposed by $\mathcal{L}_{\text{pot}}$ , we also expect $\Phi_{\theta}(\mathbf{X})$ to be spatially smooth, so we introduce a spatial smoothness loss:

$\mathcal{L}_{\text{smooth}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{X}\sim\mathcal{S}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\|\nabla\Phi_{\theta}^{i}(\mathbf{X})\|^{2},$ (8)

where $\mathcal{S}$ denotes the set of sampled cubature points introduced in Sec. , and $\nabla\Phi_{\theta}^{i}$ is the spatial gradient of the $i$ -th skinning weight function at point $\mathbf{X}$ under the current network parameters $\theta$ .

III-B

To enhance subspace expressiveness, we introduce a loss that promotes orthogonality among the learned skinning weight functions:Orthogonality Constraint.

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{orth}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}\sim\mathcal{S}}\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=1\\

j\neq i\end{subarray}}^{m}\Big(\Phi_{\theta}^{i}(\mathbf{X}_{\mathcal{D}})^{\top}\Phi_{\theta}^{j}(\mathbf{X}_{\mathcal{D}})\Big)^{2}\right],$ (9)

where $\mathcal{D}$ denotes a training batch of cubature points sampled from the overall set $\mathcal{S}$ , and $\mathbf{X}_{\mathcal{D}}$ represents the corresponding point matrix within the batch.

Simplicits  jointly penalizes deviations from orthogonality and unit magnitude. We instead $\ell_{2}$ -normalize each column of the skinning weight matrix evaluated at the batch points on the fly. This normalization regulates the scale of the learned modes and prevents numerical drift during training, thereby facilitating optimization of the orthogonality objective and promoting more independent neural skinning fields. However, gradients of the self-supervised loss terms can differ substantially in magnitude and conflict in direction, making naive joint optimization unstable. To overcome this challenge, we complement our on-the-fly skinning-field normalization with ConFIG  to correct conflicting gradients and stabilize joint optimization.

In Fig. , we visualize the evolution of different skinning modes during optimization, demonstrating that our physics-informed self-supervised framework progressively organizes the initially unstructured skinning representations into low-energy, approximately orthogonal, and spatially smooth skinning results, which are then used for real-time physics-based animation as detailed in Sec. .Stable Joint Optimization.[]

III-D

III-DSkinning-Based Real-Time Animation

The learned neural skinning fields define a continuous subspace mapping through which reduced coordinates determine full-space deformations for physics-based animation. We first describe the basic reduced dynamics, and then incorporate boundary conditions, external control, and contact energies. Rig-complementary dynamics is introduced separately in Sec. .

III-E

With the skinning-based subspace representation, we can create motions with physically plausible deformations directly in the reduced-order subspace. We discretize the governing Newtonian physical equations using standard implicit time integration and update the subspace coordinates $\mathbf{z}$ over time as:Subspace Dynamics.

$\mathbf{z}_{t+1}=\underset{\mathbf{z}}{\arg\min}\;\frac{1}{2h^{2}}\|\mathbf{z}-2\mathbf{z}_{t}+\mathbf{z}_{t-1}\|_{\mathbf{M}}^{2}+E_{\textrm{pot}}(\phi(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{z})),$ (10)

where $h$ is the time step size, $\|\cdot\|_{\mathbf{M}}$ is the norm induced by the reduced mass matrix $\mathbf{M}$ , and $E_{\textrm{pot}}$ is the potential energy that induces the internal force, with $E_{\textrm{pot}}$ supporting general hyperelastic material models. This formulation can be solved using standard Newton-based methods . The much lower subspace dimensionality allows efficient optimization of Eq. () , enabling real-time physics-based animation.[]

We extend Eq. () by augmenting its elastic potential with the energies associated with each animation setting. Let $\phi_{D}$ denote the deformation map satisfying the prescribed Dirichlet boundary conditions. For a fixed boundary displacement field and fixed constrained region, we update the reduced coordinates via:Reduced Dynamics with Control and Contact.

$\displaystyle\mathbf{z}_{t+1}=\underset{\mathbf{z}}{\arg\min}$ $\displaystyle\frac{1}{2h^{2}}\left\|\mathbf{z}-2\mathbf{z}_{t}+\mathbf{z}_{t-1}\right\|_{\mathbf{M}}^{2}+E_{\textrm{pot}}\!\left(\phi_{D}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{z})\right)$ (11) $\displaystyle+E_{\textrm{force}}(\mathbf{z},t)+E_{\textrm{bnd}}(\mathbf{z})+E_{\textrm{coll}}(\mathbf{z}).$

Here, $E_{\textrm{force}}$ accounts for the effects of gravity or user-defined actuation forces, $E_{\textrm{bnd}}$ models penalty-based environment interaction, and $E_{\textrm{coll}}$ accounts for inter-object contact. In the absence of boundary constraints, $\phi_{D}$ reduces to $\phi$ . Activating the relevant terms in Eq. () supports controllable and collision-aware animation.

11

We enforce prescribed boundary displacements through Dirichlet boundary conditions and project global or localized external forces into the reduced space to drive and interactively control object deformation.Boundary and External Control.

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}$ denote the object’s rest domain and $\Gamma_{D}\subseteq\partial\Omega$ its Dirichlet boundary. We define an indicator $d:\Omega\rightarrow\{0,1\}$ for the unconstrained region, with $d=0$ on $\Gamma_{D}$ and $d=1$ elsewhere, and let $\mathbf{g}:\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{3}$ be a displacement field that matches the prescribed displacement on $\Gamma_{D}$ . Following a boundary-compatible construction, we modify the deformation map in Eq. () as:Dirichlet Boundary Conditions.

1

$\phi_{D}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{z})=\mathbf{X}+\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{X})+d(\mathbf{X})\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bm{W}_{\!i}(\mathbf{X})\mathbf{Z}_{i}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{X}\\

1\end{bmatrix}.$ (12)

This construction is equivalent to modulating the runtime skinning fields by $d(\mathbf{X})$ . Consequently, the displacement induced by the reduced coordinates vanishes on $\Gamma_{D}$ , where $\mathbf{g}$ directly specifies the prescribed boundary displacement for arbitrary reduced coordinates. Different boundary configurations are specified by selecting different subsets of $\partial\Omega$ . As shown in Fig. (a), varying the constrained region produces distinct boundary-conditioned deformation behavior under the same reduced formulation.

4

External controls are represented as full-space force fields and then mapped to the reduced coordinates through the deformation map. Let $\bm{J}_{\phi}$ denote the Jacobian of the active deformation map with respect to the reduced coordinates. A full-space force $\mathbf{f}_{x}(t)$ gives:External Force and Interactive Control.

$\mathbf{f}_{z}(t)=\bm{J}_{\phi}^{\top}\mathbf{f}_{x}(t),\qquad E_{\textrm{force}}(\mathbf{z},t)=-\mathbf{f}_{z}(t)^{\top}\mathbf{z}.$ (13)

This linear potential applies to forces held fixed during each reduced solve. It covers global force fields, such as gravity, and localized user-defined actuation forces. Different controls share the same force-to-coordinate mapping while differing in how $\mathbf{f}_{x}(t)$ is constructed. For interactive dragging, we construct a Gaussian-kernel-weighted local force around the selected point and update the drag target position from the current user input at each frame before applying Eq. (). As shown in Fig. (b), localized dragging enables direct manipulation of different character geometries.

13

4

We handle contact through boundary-penalty environment interaction and point-based IPC-style collision energies, with the latter supporting both rigid–deformable and deformable–deformable interaction.Contact-Aware Multi-Object Dynamics.

We model simple environmental interactions, such as plane collision, as penalty constraints to prescribed geometric boundaries. Let $\Gamma_{E}$ denote an environment boundary, and let $\mathcal{A}$ be the active set of animation points within its influence region. For each active point $j$ , we compute a boundary target $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{j}\in\Gamma_{E}$ from the current environment geometry. The boundary penalty is:Boundary-Penalty Environment Interaction.

$E_{\textrm{bnd}}(\mathbf{z})=\sum_{j\in\mathcal{A}}\left\|\phi_{D}(\mathbf{X}_{j},\mathbf{z})-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{j}\right\|_{2}^{2}.$ (14)

The active set and targets are held fixed when differentiating this energy. The resulting full-space derivatives are mapped to the reduced coordinates using the same deformation-map Jacobian $\bm{J}_{\phi}$ as in Eq. (). For plane-collision scenarios, such as an inclined ramp, $\Gamma_{E}$ is instantiated as a finite rectangular boundary with a prescribed normal. The target $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{j}$ is obtained by projecting the current point onto the boundary plane and restricting it to the finite boundary extent. Moving or rotating the boundary updates its geometry, active points, and boundary targets. As shown in Fig. (c), the same boundary-penalty formulation supports contact with planar environments across diverse object geometries and boundary orientations.

13

4

Qualitative results for collision-aware multi-object animation. (a) Rigid–deformable contact between objects with distinct geometries. (b) Deformable–deformable contact among multiple objects, jointly resolved by the reduced collision formulation. Fig. 5: We encourage readers to visit our project page for additional animation videos.

For multi-object interaction, we use sampled integration points as collision primitives and construct a contact set $\mathcal{C}$ by querying neighboring points from different objects. For each contact $c$ , we store a contact direction $\mathbf{n}_{c}$ and define the contact gap $d_{c}$ as the signed separation along this direction. We normalize this gap by the contact radius $r_{c}>0$ , i.e., $\widehat{d}_{c}=d_{c}/r_{c}$ , and use the following point-based log barrier inspired by Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) :IPC-Style Collision Energy.[]

32

$E_{b,c}=\begin{cases}-(\widehat{d}_{c}-1)^{2}\log(\widehat{d}_{c}-r_{p}),&r_{p}<\widehat{d}_{c}<1,\\

0,&\widehat{d}_{c}\geq 1,\\

+\infty,&\widehat{d}_{c}\leq r_{p}.\end{cases}$ (15)

We assemble the collision term as $E_{\textrm{coll}}=k_{c}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}E_{b,c}$ , defining an IPC-style barrier over sampled point pairs. Here, $0\leq r_{p}<1$ specifies the minimum normalized contact gap, and $k_{c}$ controls the contact stiffness. The barrier is finite only for $\widehat{d}_{c}>r_{p}$ .

We model rigid-body motion with a global rigid transformation, while the deformable geometry evolves according to the neural skinning deformation map. At the beginning of each time step, the transformed rigid surface samples and current deformable points are used to construct the active contact pairs. For each pair, the point-pair barrier in Eq. () is evaluated from the contact gap between the rigid and deformable sides. The rigid transformation is treated as prescribed input to this reduced deformable solve. As shown in Fig. (a), this formulation handles rigid–deformable contact across different object pairs and motions.Rigid–Deformable Interaction.

5

For $K$ deformable objects, each object $i$ maintains its own reduced coordinates $\mathbf{z}_{i}$ , material parameters, and subspace dimension. We concatenate the reduced coordinates into the global reduced variable $\mathbf{z}=[\mathbf{z}_{1}^{\top},\ldots,\mathbf{z}_{K}^{\top}]^{\top}$ and sum the per-object inertial, elastic, and control energies. Cross-object contacts couple these states through the same point-pair barrier in Eq. (). For a contact $c$ between objects $a$ and $b$ , let $\bm{J}_{\phi,a}$ and $\bm{J}_{\phi,b}$ denote their deformation-map Jacobians with respect to $\mathbf{z}_{a}$ and $\mathbf{z}_{b}$ , respectively, evaluated at the corresponding contact points. With the contact direction and radius held fixed during differentiation, the contact gap is affine in $\mathbf{z}$ . Applying the chain rule to the barrier energy gives the following reduced derivatives, showing only the nonzero blocks for objects $a$ and $b$ :Deformable–Deformable Interaction.

15

$\displaystyle\bm{J}_{c}$ $\displaystyle=\frac{\partial d_{c}}{\partial\mathbf{z}}=\mathbf{n}_{c}^{\top}[\,\bm{J}_{\phi,a}\;-\bm{J}_{\phi,b}\,],$ (16) $\displaystyle\nabla_{\mathbf{z}}E_{b,c}$ $\displaystyle=\bm{J}_{c}^{\top}\frac{\partial E_{b,c}}{\partial d_{c}},\qquad\nabla_{\mathbf{z}}^{2}E_{b,c}=\bm{J}_{c}^{\top}\frac{\partial^{2}E_{b,c}}{\partial d_{c}^{2}}\bm{J}_{c}.$

At each reduced solve step, we assemble these per-contact derivatives into the global gradient and Hessian of $E_{\textrm{coll}}(\mathbf{z})$ , directly coupling the reduced states of contacting objects. As shown in Fig. (b), the resulting coupled system jointly resolves contacts among multiple deformable objects.

III-ERig-Complementary Animation

Beyond purely physics-driven animation, PhysSkin++ also supports rig-complementary animation when an artist-authored LBS rig is available. The prescribed rig deformation serves as the primary animation, while complementary elastic deformation is parameterized by reduced coordinates through the learned neural skinning fields. We first describe the rig-based deformation and then introduce the rig-space complementarity objective used during self-supervised learning.

Consider a skeletal rig with $n_{\mathrm{b}}$ bones, pose parameters $\mathbf{p}$ , and rest pose $\mathbf{p}^{0}$ . Let $\mathbf{G}_{b}(\mathbf{p})\in\mathrm{SE}(3)$ be the global transformation of bone $b$ , obtained by composing its local transformations along the kinematic hierarchy. We denote by $\mathbf{A}_{b}(\mathbf{p})\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 4}$ the affine transform induced by the relative bone motion $\mathbf{G}_{b}(\mathbf{p})\mathbf{G}_{b}(\mathbf{p}^{0})^{-1}$ . With rig skinning weights $\bm{W}_{b}^{\mathrm{rig}}(\mathbf{X})$ , LBS  maps a rest-space point as:Rig-Based Deformation Representation.[]

43

$\phi_{\mathrm{rig}}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{p})=\sum_{b=1}^{n_{\mathrm{b}}}\bm{W}_{b}^{\mathrm{rig}}(\mathbf{X})\mathbf{A}_{b}(\mathbf{p})\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{X}\\

1\end{bmatrix}.$ (17)

Here, $\mathbf{A}_{b}(\mathbf{p})$ moves the point from the rest configuration according to bone $b$ , and the weighted sum blends the bone-transformed positions. Subtracting the rest position gives the rig displacement $\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{rig}}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{p})=\phi_{\mathrm{rig}}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{p})-\mathbf{X}$ . This formulation is efficient and directly controllable, but its kinematic deformations alone cannot produce physical elastic responses.

For rig-complementary animation, we augment the representation in Eq. () with the prescribed rig displacement:

1

$\displaystyle\phi(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{p},\mathbf{z})=$ $\displaystyle\mathbf{X}+\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{rig}}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{p})$ (18) $\displaystyle+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bm{W}_{\theta,i}^{\mathrm{comp}}(\mathbf{X})\mathbf{Z}_{i}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{X}\\

1\end{bmatrix}.$

The neural skinning term defines the complementary elastic displacement $\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{comp}}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{z})$ . Both animation settings share the continuous skinning parameterization, with rig-complementary animation incorporating the prescribed rig displacement.

Fig.  summarizes our self-supervised rig-complementarity training pipeline.Rig-Space Complementarity Constraint.

Self-supervised rig-complementarity training. The rig Jacobian of a prescribed rig provides a complementarity constraint for learning rig-complementary neural skinning fields from static geometry.Fig. 6:

For a batch $\mathcal{D}$ of $N_{\mathcal{D}}$ cubature points, we stack the rig and complementary displacements as $\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{rig}}(\mathbf{p}),\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{comp}}(\mathbf{z})\in\mathbb{R}^{3N_{\mathcal{D}}}$ . We denote the rig Jacobian by $\bm{J}_{\mathrm{rig}}=\partial\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{rig}}(\mathbf{p})/\partial\mathbf{p}$ . To prevent the physical component from duplicating motion expressible by the rig, we seek complementary displacements satisfying:

$\bm{J}_{\mathrm{rig}}^{\top}\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{comp}}=\mathbf{0}.$ (19)

This condition makes the complementary displacement orthogonal to the rig motion subspace spanned by the columns of $\bm{J}_{\mathrm{rig}}$ under the Euclidean inner product.

To impose this condition for arbitrary subspace coordinates $\mathbf{z}$ , we arrange the batch point matrix as $\mathbf{X}_{\mathcal{D}}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times N_{\mathcal{D}}}$ and collect the predicted complementary weights in $\bm{W}_{\theta}^{\mathrm{comp}}(\mathbf{X}_{\mathcal{D}})\in\mathbb{R}^{N_{\mathcal{D}}\times m}$ . Consistent with Eq. (), the corresponding discrete skinning matrix is constructed as:

18

$\displaystyle\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{lbs}}^{\mathrm{comp}}$ $\displaystyle=\mathbf{I}_{3}\otimes\Bigg[\left(\mathbf{1}_{m}^{\top}\otimes\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{X}_{\mathcal{D}}\\

\mathbf{1}_{N_{\mathcal{D}}}^{\top}\end{bmatrix}^{\top}\right)$ (20) $\displaystyle\odot\left(\bm{W}_{\theta}^{\mathrm{comp}}(\mathbf{X}_{\mathcal{D}})\otimes\mathbf{1}_{4}^{\top}\right)\Bigg].$

Here, $\otimes$ and $\odot$ denote the Kronecker and Hadamard products, respectively, and $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{lbs}}^{\mathrm{comp}}\in\mathbb{R}^{3N_{\mathcal{D}}\times 12m}$ . The displacement stacking and the flattening of handle parameters use the ordering consistent with this matrix, so that $\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{comp}}=\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{lbs}}^{\mathrm{comp}}\mathbf{z}$ .

We use a linear control parameterization of the prescribed rig, yielding a constant rig Jacobian $\bm{J}_{\mathrm{rig}}$  . Since $\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{comp}}=\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{lbs}}^{\mathrm{comp}}\mathbf{z}$ , the complementarity condition in Eq. () holds for arbitrary $\mathbf{z}$ when:[]

6

19

$\bm{J}_{\mathrm{rig}}^{\top}\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{lbs}}^{\mathrm{comp}}=\mathbf{0}.$ (21)

We optimize the predicted complementary skinning weights using the following rig-space complementarity loss:

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comp}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{R})}\left[\left\|\bm{J}_{\mathrm{rig}}^{\top}\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{lbs}}^{\mathrm{comp}}\right\|_{F}^{2}\right],$ (22)

where $\mathcal{R}$ denotes the prescribed rig and its Jacobian is evaluated on the same batch points as $\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{lbs}}^{\mathrm{comp}}$ . The rig-complementary training objective augments Eq. ():

6

$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rig}}(\theta)=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{subspace}}(\theta)+\lambda_{\mathrm{comp}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comp}}(\theta),$ (23)

where $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{subspace}}$ is the self-supervised subspace learning objective defined in Eq. (), $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comp}}$ is the rig-space complementarity loss defined in Eq. (), and $\lambda_{\mathrm{comp}}$ is a weighting hyperparameter. We optimize the resulting objective using the on-the-fly skinning-field normalization and conflict-aware gradient correction described in Sec. .

At runtime, the deformation representation in Eq. () expresses object deformation through the prescribed rig displacement and a complementary elastic displacement parameterized by the reduced coordinates. The rig trajectory $\{\mathbf{p}_{t}\}$ is supplied as an external kinematic input, such as an animator-authored pose sequence. Given the prescribed pose $\mathbf{p}_{t+1}$ , we update the complementary coordinates through implicit reduced dynamics:Rig-Driven Complementary Dynamics.

18

$\displaystyle\mathbf{z}_{t+1}$ $\displaystyle=\underset{\mathbf{z}}{\arg\min}\;\frac{1}{2h^{2}}\left\|\mathbf{z}-2\mathbf{z}_{t}+\mathbf{z}_{t-1}\right\|_{\mathbf{M}}^{2}$ (24) $\displaystyle+E_{\textrm{pot}}\!\left(\mathbf{X}+\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{comp}}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{z})+\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{rig}}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{p}_{t+1})\right).$

The complementarity loss in Eq. () encourages the condition in Eq. () during training, allowing the runtime solve to optimize only the complementary coordinates without additional complementarity constraints. As shown in Fig. , this formulation supports both interactive rig control and user-authored rig animation sequences, enriching their kinematic deformation with physics-based complementary elastic response.

III-FDiscretization-Agnostic Animation Binding

A key advantage of representing skinning weights as continuous neural fields is the resulting discretization-agnostic deformation map. The learned fields can be evaluated directly at mesh vertices, sampled points, and neural scene primitives, allowing the same reduced physical state to deform different spatial discretizations. We demonstrate this binding capability with 3D Gaussian Splatting by directly binding the anisotropic Gaussian primitives to the learned skinning fields.

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)  represents a scene using anisotropic Gaussian primitives $\mathcal{G}=\{\mathcal{G}_{g}\}_{g=1}^{N_{G}}$ , each parameterized as:3D Gaussian Representation.[]

28

$\mathcal{G}_{g}=\left\{\bm{\mu}_{g},\,\mathbf{R}_{g},\,\mathbf{s}_{g},\,\alpha_{g},\,\mathbf{c}_{g}\right\},$ (25)

where $\bm{\mu}_{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ is the center, $\mathbf{R}_{g}\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is the rotation matrix, $\mathbf{s}_{g}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{3}$ contains the principal-axis scales, $\alpha_{g}\in[0,1]$ is the opacity, and $\mathbf{c}_{g}$ denotes the spherical harmonic (SH) appearance coefficients. The corresponding 3D covariance matrix is:

$\Sigma_{g}=\mathbf{R}_{g}\mathbf{S}_{g}\mathbf{S}_{g}^{\top}\mathbf{R}_{g}^{\top},\qquad\mathbf{S}_{g}=\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf{s}_{g}).$ (26)

For rendering, each 3D Gaussian is projected to a screen-space Gaussian, whose color contribution is accumulated through depth-ordered alpha blending. Animating the Gaussian representation therefore requires updating the center and covariance of each Gaussian according to the underlying physical deformation.

Let $\bm{\mu}_{g}^{0}$ denote the rest center of the $g$ -th Gaussian. Since the neural skinning fields are spatially continuous, we directly evaluate $\bm{W}_{i}(\bm{\mu}_{g}^{0})$ at its rest center. Following the deformation map in Eq. (), we construct the local affine transformation for each Gaussian as:Continuous Gaussian Binding.

1

$\mathbf{T}_{g}(\mathbf{z})\equiv\left[\mathbf{A}_{g}(\mathbf{z})\;\mathbf{t}_{g}(\mathbf{z})\right]=\left[\mathbf{I}_{3}\;\mathbf{0}\right]+\sum_{i=1}^{m}\bm{W}_{\!i}(\bm{\mu}_{g}^{0})\mathbf{Z}_{i},$ (27)

where $\mathbf{A}_{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}$ is the linear part of the affine transformation, which may include rotation, scaling, and shear, and $\mathbf{t}_{g}\in\mathbb{R}^{3}$ is its translation. We evaluate the skinning weights once at each Gaussian’s rest center and use these fixed weights throughout its kernel. The resulting local affine transformation is updated from the current reduced coordinates.

Let $\Sigma_{g}^{0}$ denote the rest covariance. Applying the local affine transformation $\mathbf{T}_{g}(\mathbf{z})$ to the Gaussian kernel gives:Gaussian Kernel Deformation.

$\displaystyle\bm{\mu}_{g}(\mathbf{z})$ $\displaystyle=\mathbf{A}_{g}(\mathbf{z})\bm{\mu}_{g}^{0}+\mathbf{t}_{g}(\mathbf{z}),$ (28) $\displaystyle\Sigma_{g}(\mathbf{z})$ $\displaystyle=\mathbf{A}_{g}(\mathbf{z})\Sigma_{g}^{0}\mathbf{A}_{g}(\mathbf{z})^{\top}.$

The center therefore follows the skinned point motion, while the covariance captures the induced rotation and anisotropic deformation of the Gaussian kernel. The opacity and SH coefficients retain their rest values.

At runtime, we advance the reduced coordinates $\mathbf{z}$ using Eq. (). At each frame, these coordinates determine the local affine maps in Eq. (), which update the Gaussian centers and covariances through Eq. (), driving physics-based animation of the Gaussian representation.Runtime Coupling.

IV Experiments

IV-AImplementation Details

For the 3D shape encoder, we adopt the pre-trained Michelangelo  model which consists of one cross-attention block and eight self-attention blocks; the output latent set $\mathbf{F}_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d}$ has $M=256$ and $d=768$ . For each 3D object, we re-center and normalize it into a bounding volume of $[-1,1]^{3}$ . For the 3D shape encoder, we sample 4096 points on the object surface as input. For cubature points sampling, we first sample 100k points on the surface, and then voxelize the space into a $128^{3}$ grid to obtain interior points to form the complete candidate cubature point set. For each training batch, we randomly sample 1000 cubature points from the candidate point set for potential energy computation, following the same strategy as previous work . In each batch, we randomly sample 1024 subspace coordinate vectors $\mathbf{z}$ for training. Our framework is trained on 4 NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPUs. The learning rate is linearly increased to $5\times 10^{-4}$ within the first $1\%$ of training iterations (warm-up), and then gradually decreased using the cosine decay schedule until reaching the minimum value of $5\times 10^{-5}$ .[]

Since our framework is entirely self-supervised and does not rely on annotated skinning data as ground truth, we draw from matrix analysis  and spectral theory  to propose three quantitative metrics that measure ,

To ensure a fair comparison, we perform $\ell_{2}$ -normalization on each column of $W$ before evaluation for all methods, resulting in the matrix $\hat{W}$ .Evaluation Metrics.[, ]

We first measure the pairwise orthogonality among handle or bone influence vectors as:(1) Orthogonality Metric.

$\Omega_{\text{orth}}=\frac{1}{K(K-1)}\|\,\hat{W}^{\top}\hat{W}-I\,\|_{2}^{2},$ (29)

where $I$ is the $K\times K$ identity matrix. A smaller $\Omega_{\text{orth}}$ indicates that different handle or bone weights are more decorrelated and capture distinct deformation subspaces. Since each column of $\hat{W}$ is $\ell_{2}$ -normalized, $\Omega_{\text{orth}}$ is bounded within $[0,1]$ ,

and a smaller value indicates that each handle or bone encodes an independent deformation mode.

To evaluate the numerical stability of the skinning basis, we compute the log-scaled condition number  of the Gram matrix:(2) Log-Condition Number Metric.[]

21

$\kappa_{\log}=\log_{2}\Big(1+\frac{\lambda_{\max}(\hat{W}^{\top}\hat{W})}{\lambda_{\min}(\hat{W}^{\top}\hat{W})}\Big),$ (30)

where $\lambda_{\max}$ and $\lambda_{\min}$ are the largest and smallest eigenvalues of $\hat{W}^{\top}\hat{W}$ .

$\kappa_{\log}$ lies within $[1,+\infty)$ ; a smaller value indicates a well-conditioned deformation basis, where small transformations result in stable geometric responses.

To assess the balance of spectral energy distribution across skinning weights, we define the spectrum entropy metric  as:(3) Spectrum Entropy Metric.[, ]

13

54

$H_{\text{spec}}=-\frac{1}{\log K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}p_{i}\log p_{i},\;p_{i}=\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\sum_{j}\lambda_{j}},$ (31)

where $\{\lambda_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K}$ are the eigenvalues of $\hat{W}^{\top}\hat{W}$ . $H_{\text{spec}}$ is bounded within $[0,1]$ , where

higher values indicate more uniform spectral energy and balanced, expressive deformation modes.

IV-CAblation Studies

To validate our design choices, we conduct ablation studies covering both the key components of the proposed Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning (PISSL) strategy and the rig-space complementarity term in the rig-complementary setting, using the RigNet  dataset. As shown in Table , we remove or modify the PISSL components to assess their individual effects on model performance. Specifically, we evaluate the smoothness loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{smooth}}$ , the orthogonality constraint $\mathcal{L}_{\text{orth}}$ , the skinning normalization process, the ONI  layer, and conflict-aware gradient correction using ConFIG . The quantitative results demonstrate that these components maintain the numerical stability and orthogonality of the learned neural skinning fields, which are essential for well-conditioned and physically consistent deformation behavior. In Fig. , we visualize the skinning results obtained without the potential energy loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{pot}}$ , where the model fails to produce physically interpretable skinning fields. Fig.  further compares neural skinning fields learned with and without $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comp}}$ . Without this term, the visualized fields form broad regions across the head, torso, and limbs. Incorporating $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{comp}}$ changes these distributions, with visible differences in the ears, wings, and limb regions across multiple characters. These comparisons illustrate the effect of rig-space complementarity learning on the spatial organization of the skinning fields.[]

V Conclusion

In this paper, we present PhysSkin++, a generalizable physics-informed framework for real-time physics-based animation across diverse 3D shapes and discretizations. A neural skinning fields autoencoder learns continuous skinning fields directly from static geometries to define a skinning-based subspace mapping. Our Physics-Informed Self-Supervised Learning (PISSL) strategy promotes physically plausible deformations through a self-supervised objective and stabilizes joint optimization through on-the-fly skinning-field normalization and conflict-aware gradient correction. At runtime, a reduced dynamics formulation advances the reduced coordinates and supports Dirichlet boundary conditions, interactive control, environmental interaction, and both rigid–deformable and deformable–deformable contact. Beyond purely physics-driven animation, we extend the deformation representation with prescribed rig displacement and the self-supervised objective with a rig-space complementarity term, enabling complementary elastic responses for prescribed rig animations without enforcing the complementarity constraint at runtime. The continuous deformation map also enables discretization-agnostic binding to meshes, point clouds, and 3D Gaussian representations. Experiments demonstrate that PhysSkin++ achieves outstanding performance on generalizable neural skinning while enabling real-time physics-based animation. As a limitation, our current formulation does not incorporate semantic priors for modeling complex geometries. Future work will explore such priors to improve the expressiveness of the learned skinning-based subspace mapping.

item.title: 皮克斯《Hoppers》的制作幕后搬上 SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 ｜ Pixar Animation Studios Brings the Making of 'Hoppers' to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026
item.description:
一句话：皮克斯将在 SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 分享新片《Hoppers》的创意决策与技术实现。

要点：

  • 聚焦创意选择如何反向驱动技术方案，而非单列技术清单
  • 披露影片制作中动画与渲染管线的新增模块
  • SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 现场场次，会后通常有幻灯片与论文流出

为什么值得看：顶级动画工作室的管线演进往往会下沉到引擎，提前知道他们解决了什么问题，可以少走弯路。

中文摘要：SIGGRAPH 官方博客预告了皮克斯在 SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 的场次：围绕新片《Hoppers》讲述制作过程中的创意决策、技术创新与团队协作。文章强调创意需求如何倒逼技术选型，而不是罗列工具。对关注动画管线、角色渲染与制作流程的开发者来说，这是每年少有的能直接听到一线工作室复盘的机会。

主题：图形学

来源：SIGGRAPH Blog（English）

Pixar Animation Studios Brings the Making of ‘Hoppers’ to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026

by | | ,

SIGGRAPH Asia

15 October 2026

Animation

Conferences

Image credit: Leading image provided by SIGGRAPH Asia 2026

This December, the creative minds behind Disney and Pixar’s “Hoppers” are heading to Kuala Lumpur!

SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 is excited to welcome Pixar Animation Studios for a Featured Speakers session, “We’re All In This Together: The Making Of Disney and Pixar’s ‘Hoppers,’” offering a behind-the-scenes look at the artistry, technology, and collaboration that brought the film to life.

Creating the world of “Hoppers” came with a unique challenge: Bringing together three distinct visual styles, from the graphic clarity of comedy and the carefully controlled lighting and staging of suspense to the rich, observational beauty of nature photography.

To bring these elements together, the filmmakers developed a collaborative approach that balanced stylization with realism, combining physical simulation and artistic design to create the film’s distinctive visual world.

At SIGGRAPH Asia 2026, the Pixar team will share insights into the creative decisions, technical innovations, and collaborative processes behind the film, highlighting how artists and technologists across different disciplines worked together to bring their vision to the screen.

Meet the Pixar Team at SIGGRAPH Asia 2026

Layout lead, Pixar Animation Studios VFX supervisor, Pixar Animation Studios Tailoring and simulation supervisor, Pixar Animation StudiosAndrea Goh,Beth Albright,Lyon Liew,

More Exciting Program Highlights to Come!

And that’s not all! More exciting sessions, industry-leading speakers, and program highlights are still to be announced as we count down to SIGGRAPH Asia 2026.

Stay tuned to the as we continue to unveil what’s in store this December!

SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 website

Don’t Miss Out — Secure Your Pass Today!

📅 📍 1-4 December 2026Kuala Lumpur Convention Centre, Malaysia

Secure your place today and join the global community as we come together to .Weave the Future
